\(10\) One of the best forward-looking clues on where the economy and
certain industries are headed can be found in this detailed table. One
cannot overstate the value of information provided here. For example,
one statistic worth tracking for clues about future employment measures
shifts in the hiring of temporary workers. Keep in mind that temp work
has become an increasingly important segment of the labor economy
because it allows companies to operate with greater flexibility. More
than 25% of all new positions filled by business in 2010 were temporary
jobs. Fifteen years earlier, temp employment accounted for just 6% of
all new private-sector jobs. The reason one should carefully monitor the
temporary workforce is that it also serves as an excellent forecasting
tool. Temps are the first to lose their jobs when an economy gets into
trouble, a trend that can begin as early as 12 months before the onset
of recession. Once the economy makes the important turn from recession
to recovery—a transition that is difficult to identify in real
time—businesses will prefer to employ temporary help first before taking
the more expensive step of permanently hiring and training new full-time
employees. Once employers <span id="ch03a.html_page_47"></span>trust
that the recovery is real, they feel more comfortable about recruiting
permanent workers. (In addition to the Bureau of Labor Statistics
monthly numbers on temp employment, a weekly measure can be found at the
American Staffing Association’s Web site,
*[www.americanstaffing.net/statistics/staffing_index.cfm](http://www.americanstaffing.net/statistics/staffing_index.cfm)*.)

A second great metric to follow is employment in “truck transportation.”
The demand for truck drivers is highly sensitive to booms and busts in
the economic cycle. If retailers and manufacturers sense that demand is
slacking or see their inventories swelling, they will reduce new orders
from their own suppliers. Since most basic commodities and finished
consumer products get shipped to their final destination by trucks, a
decline in orders will reduce demand for truck drivers and even lead to
layoffs. On the other hand, if customer demand improves and inventories
get too thin, new orders will rebound and that increases the need for
truckers.

A third useful data point is to track monthly swings in employment in
the “child-care services” industry. As conditions in the job market
improve, the number of working parents increases and they will make
arrangements to place their young children with child-care centers. Many
states have strict laws on the ratio of teachers to infants and
toddlers, which means these centers will be obligated to hire more
people to be in legal compliance. Should economic conditions deteriorate
and layoffs accelerate, child-care centers will see demand for their
service decline, and this has typically led to dismissals of caretakers.

#### Market Impact

##### Bonds

Traders get quite agitated when there’s a strong jobs report, especially
if it’s unexpected. The news can portend accelerating inflation and
rising interest rates, both of which are anathema to bondholders. Thus,
be prepared for a sell-off in fixed-income securities when job creation
is surging. How far bond prices will fall and how much yields will rise
depends on many factors, but the most important is where the economy
happens to be in the business cycle. If the U.S. has just managed to
climb out of recession, a jump in employment will likely have only a
modest effect on bond prices, because there’s no immediate danger of
inflation. However, if employment accelerates when the economy is
already operating at or near peak capacity, prepare to see a steep drop
in bond prices and sharply higher interest rates.

In contrast, a series of weak employment reports reflects a more
sluggish economy, which is bullish for bond prices and means interest
rates will head lower.

##### <span id="ch03a.html_page_48"></span>Stocks

News of robust employment can make equity investors positively giddy. As
the number of people holding jobs increases and the workweek expands,
employees easily slip into the role of consumers and spend more money.
The result: Expectations rise that business sales and profits will pick
up in the future. This can set the stage for a rally in the equity
market. The only exception is if the economy is overheating, with
interest rates and inflation turning up. The higher cost of borrowing
will hurt companies and undermine stock prices.

Little or no growth in employment is generally seen as bad for stocks.
The worry is that households will be less inclined to shop. Weak sales
can shrink corporate income and earnings, thereby reducing the incentive
to own shares.

##### Dollar

Employment news can greatly influence the dollar’s value in currency
markets. A vigorous jobs report could drive interest rates higher and
rally stocks, which makes the dollar more attractive to foreign
investors. They can now earn more interest income by owning U.S.
Treasury securities and gain from higher equity values. On the other
hand, an anemic jobs report softens demand for U.S. currency, because it
spells trouble for American stocks and puts downward pressure on rates,
both of which make the dollar less appealing to foreigners.

### <span id="ch03a.html_page_49"></span>Job Openings and Labor Turnover

**Market Sensitivity:** Low.

**What Is It** The report captures the churning that takes place in the
labor market. It publishes the the total number of new hires and layoffs
in the month, as well as how many job openings remained in that period.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/jolts.pdf](http://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/jolts.pdf)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.bls.gov](http://www.bls.gov)*

**Release Time:** 10:00 a.m. (ET); published about five to six weeks
after the reference month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor.

**Revisions:** With each release, the government makes revisions to the
previous month, though they tend to be minor. Benchmark revisions are
done once a year, usually in March, and can go back two years.

#### Why Is It Important?

You might have taken notice that we began this chapter with the most
anxiously awaited economic report of the entire month: the Employment
Situation report. But even that major market-moving indicator lacks some
vital information about what is happening on the job front. For example,
the Employment Situation report says *nothing* about how many people
were actually hired in the latest month. Nor does it tell us the number
of jobs eliminated. Surprised? All the headline statistic in the main
Employment Situation report (aside from the unemployment rate) is just
the month-to month “change” in the number of people on corporate and
government payrolls, which is simply the “net” difference between the
number of jobs created and the number of jobs eliminated. That’s it! So
if the government announces that payrolls increased by 250,000 in a
particular month, that figure merely reflects the difference in the
aggregate number of new hires, less all the jobs that were lost. What
you don’t see is the actual “gross” number of positions filled and
eliminated.

Why are the gross numbers so important? There is no better measure of
the economy’s health than its ability to create new positions. And the
fact is that the U.S. economy actually generates far more jobs than most
of us think. How much more? This may surprise you. On average, 4 million
to 5 million new positions are filled *every single month* in sectors
like construction, manufacturing, retail, services, and the government.
Even during the lowest point of the 2008–09 Great Recession—when the
Employment Situation reported horrific “net” job losses month after
month—another less-well-known economic indicator showed that more than
3.5 million new positions were filled during
<span id="ch03a.html_page_50"></span>those same months. The problem was
that an even greater number of jobs disappeared, which accounts for the
net figure showing large losses in payrolls.

For us to really understand what is going on in the labor market, we
have to follow not only the Employment Situation release but also its
lesser-known cousin with the awkward title of “[Job Openings and Labor
Turnover](#ch03a.html_ch03alev1sec2),” often referred to by its acronym
as the JOLT report. What makes the JOLT report so useful to investors,
business leaders, and policymakers is that it provides a fuller picture
of the churning that occurs in the workforce.

#### How Is It Computed?

The government’s Bureau of Labor Statistics breaks down the JOLT numbers
into three main sections: job openings, hires, and separations (and the
last of these is further differentiated by quits, layoffs, and
discharges). To get data on each section, the BLS randomly contacts
16,000 non-farm business establishments each month from a universe of
9.1 million firms. The sample covers factories, offices, and retailers,
as well as federal, state, and local government agencies in all 50
states. Questionnaires about job market activity are sent out and the
answers come back by telephone, fax, e-mail, or regular mail, or via
Web-based responses.

Based on the survey responses, the BLS presents the data in the
following format:

*Job Openings:* It represents the number of jobs available on the last
day of each month. These are positions that firms are actively
recruiting from outside the company. It makes no difference whether the
positions are full-time, part-time, temporary, or permanent. All are
included.

*Hires:* This is the total number of positions filled that entire month.

*Separations:* The column aggregates the number of jobs eliminated
during the entire month. However, there are several subgroups in this
category, since “separations” can happen for a number of reasons. They
can occur because of *layoffs and discharges,* both of which are
involuntary dismissals. (Layoffs and discharges are often the result of
mergers, downsizing, or closings, or for a specific cause, such as
employee theft.) *Quits* are when employees voluntarily chose to
terminate their employment. People might quit because of dissatisfaction
with their work or because they are hopeful of getting better employment
opportunities elsewhere. The final subgroup is called *Other
Separations,* which covers retirements, deaths, and those who left due
to disability.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_51"></span>The Tables: Clues on What’s Ahead for the Economy

The JOLT report is a fairly new series with data going back no further
than December 2000. Nevertheless, it has already shown some usefulness
as a forecasting tool.

<span id="ch03a.html_ch03atab09"></span>Table A. Job Openings, Hires,
and Total Separations by Industry, Seasonally Adjusted

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/03sei10.jpg)

</div>

\(1\) This column reflects the total the number of job openings and
their origins—the private sector and government. The data can serve as
an important analytical tool for economists and investors since it tells
us something about the demand for workers, how it changes month to
month, and in what industries. In many ways it represents the ultimate
gauge of how optimistic (or worried) employers are about the economic
outlook, since labor is the costliest investment companies make.

Where it gets interesting is that the number of job openings turns
markedly lower well in advance of when an economy slips into recession.
For example, job openings peaked nine months before the U.S. economy
turned down in December 2007. This trend of hitting a high and then
plummeting long before a recession commences also occurred in 2001,
following the dot.com bust. It is a pattern that is likely to be
repeated in future business cycles because firms are highly sensitive to
a softening in demand for goods and services and will quickly pull back
on job postings.

\(2\) Hires: Here we have the total number of positions filled that
month. It also is broken down by sectors. As noted previously with job
openings, companies will typically slow the pace of hiring if they
suspect that the economy is losing steam. Just how sensitive is this
metric to downswings in business activity? The number of hires peaked
more than a year before the beginning of the 2008–09 recession. Although
the series on “hires” hasn’t been around for very long, there is some
empirical evidence of its value as a predictive tool.

\(3\) Separations: This column contains the total count of separations,
which includes quits, layoffs, discharges, and other reasons for
separations. It tells us little about the economy since embedded in this
category are two contradictory messages. For example, a surge in large
layoffs and discharges can certainly warn of rising economic problems.
On the other hand, a big jump in the number of quits typically portends
just the opposite. In a more vibrant economy, where jobs are more
plentiful, dissatisfied workers might be more willing to quit one job
and seek another. To better understand what is behind these separation
numbers, we go to [Tables B](#ch03a.html_ch03atab10) and C.

<span id="ch03a.html_page_52"></span><span id="ch03a.html_ch03atab10"></span>Table
B. Layoffs and Discharges, Seasonally Adjusted

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/03sei11.jpg)

</div>

\(4\) An acceleration in layoffs and discharges can cut household
spending and hurt the economy. Conversely, a sustained decline in these
numbers can boost consumer confidence and encourage more shopping.
Having said that, it is important to add that there can be a lot of
noise in this series. Layoffs can occur in large numbers throughout the
business cycles as firms merge, go out of business, outsource to foreign
countries, and downsize. Correctly interpreting a trend here requires
that it be corroborated with other economic indicators, such as those
found in [Table 4](#ch03a.html_ch03atab11), as well as changes in
applications for unemployment insurance (page
[55](#ch03a.html_page_55)).

<span id="ch03a.html_page_53"></span><span id="ch03a.html_ch03atab11"></span>Table
4. Quit Levels and Rates by Industry and Region, Seasonally Adjusted

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/03sei12.jpg)

</div>

\(5\) One can obtain a more accurate assessment on current economic
conditions by monitoring the size of quits over time. As you can
imagine, employees, no matter how unhappy they might be at their work,
are reluctant to walk away from their jobs and risk losing income if the
labor market is awful. The propensity to quit is naturally much greater
in a growing economy where employment opportunities are brighter. Thus
the quit numbers tend to be highest during periods of robust economic
activity and lowest during a recession when employers are not in a
hiring mood.

That’s why the levels of quits and job openings often move in tandem.
For instance, the number of workers who voluntarily left their job
started to decline about a year before the onset of the 2008–09
recession, and did not pick up again until well after the recovery had
started.

One last point: Some people may wonder what the difference is between
the quit levels in the JOLT report and the number of “job leavers” in
the Employment Situation release. Both count how many people have opted
out of their jobs. The answer is that they come from different sources.
The monthly figure on “job leavers” is based on inquiries made to
households, whereas the level of quits reflects responses from firms.
Which is a more accurate reflection of such departures? Understandably,
the quit numbers in the JOLT report portray a more reliable picture of
labor-market turnover, in part because some individuals in the household
survey may be reluctant to admit to being laid off and prefer instead to
say they left of their own accord.

• Ratio of Unemployed to Job Openings (No Chart)

One useful metric that is not found in this report but can easily be
calculated is to determine how many unemployed workers are competing for
each job opening. Let’s assume that the number of unemployed in the
labor force (as listed in Summary [Table A](#ch03a.html_ch03atab09) of
the Employment Situation release) came to 14 million. At the same time,
the JOLT report’s [Table A](#ch03a.html_ch03atab09) noted that there
were 3 million job openings. This tells us there are about 5 unemployed
individuals vying for each job opening. By tracking this ratio over
time, we can see whether labor-market conditions are getting better or
worse. In the five years prior to the 2008–09 recession, the ratio of
job seekers to available positions averaged 2:1, which means there were
two jobless people for every open position. But that ratio jumped to
nearly 7:1 in the spring of 2009 when the recession was at its worst.
While this entire series is relatively new, it appears that during
periods of healthy economic growth, the ratio settles in the range of
2:1 to 3:1. When the <span id="ch03a.html_page_54"></span>ratio moves
above 4:1, however, it serves as another warning that economic growth
has slowed and that labor-market conditions are tightening. This will
have repercussions for household spending in the months ahead.

#### Market Impact

##### Bonds

By the time this report comes out, a dozen other job-related surveys for
the same reference period have already been released. As a result, bond
traders do not react much to the publication of the JOLT series.

##### Stocks

Investors in the equity market take a different approach. Although JOLT
won’t ignite much new trading, there is increasing interest in what this
report says about the total number of hires, job openings, and level of
quits. This information is not available elsewhere and can thus add to
our knowledge of current economic conditions and how it might affect
revenues and earnings with specific industries.

##### Dollar

There is no measurable reaction from currency traders to the JOLT
report.

### <span id="ch03a.html_page_55"></span>Weekly Claims for Unemployment Insurance

**Market Sensitivity:** High.

**What Is It:** Tracks new filings for unemployment insurance benefits.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.ows.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims_arch.asp](http://www.ows.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims_arch.asp)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.ows.doleta.gov](http://www.ows.doleta.gov)*

**Release Time:** 8:30 a.m. (ET) every Thursday; covers the week ending
the previous Saturday.

**Frequency:** Weekly.

**Source:** Employment and Training Administration, Department of Labor.

**Revisions:** Minor changes.

#### Why Is It Important?

Experts have paid closer attention to this indicator in the past few
years even though it has been around since 1967. Improved monitoring by
the Labor Department has made the series more accurate in gauging
labor-market conditions. The main appeal of the jobless claims report is
its timeliness. Figures on new filings for unemployment benefits are
released every week and are based on actual reports from state agencies
around the country. As a result, analysts view this statistic as a good
coincident indicator, meaning it accurately reflects what is presently
going on in the economy. However, its greatest value is how first-time
claims for unemployment insurance can influence future economic
activity. If a large number of people are losing their jobs every week
and applying for unemployment compensation, this will eventually dampen
consumer spirits, slash their spending, and cause business to pare back
investments. For this reason, the weekly claims report for unemployment
benefits is one of the components in the forward-looking Index of
Leading Economic Indicators. (See the section “[Index of Leading
Economic Indicators \[LEI\]](#ch03c.html_ch03clev1sec4),” later in this
chapter.)

But let’s take a step back for a moment. What exactly do we mean by “new
claims for unemployment benefits”? Whether the economy is growing or
not, it’s a fact of life that people lose jobs every day. Companies
close money-losing factories, get bought out by competitors, outsource
to other countries, and in some instances just go belly up. Many of
their former employees are eligible to collect unemployment insurance
for as long as 26 weeks in most states. Occasionally, laws are passed
that extend the benefit period. The real issue, however, is that if the
number of people filing for unemployment benefits increases every week
or remains at a high level, it’s a worrying sign that the economy is
ailing. In contrast, a sustained decline in initial claims for benefits
points to an economy on the mend.

<span id="ch03a.html_page_56"></span>In addition to counting new filers
for benefit payments, this report also keeps tabs on the overall number
of jobless workers who are receiving state unemployment benefits, a
category known as “insured unemployment.” It’s important to point out
that not everyone who is jobless is entitled to unemployment benefits.
Labor economists estimate that more than 10% of initial claim
applications for benefits are rejected because they do not meet
eligibility requirements. In some industries, such as agriculture, as
many as half of those who have lost jobs don’t qualify for such
benefits. Recent graduates who have entered the workforce but are unable
to find employment are also ineligible to receive benefit payments.
Moreover, not all states have the same eligibility requirements; some
are stricter than others. What all this means is that many who are
unemployed receive no benefits at all. During 2011, 14 million people
were without jobs, according to the household survey of the employment
report. But less than half of them actually collected state unemployment
benefits. That’s an enormous gap, one that can have significant social
and economic consequences over time.

#### How Is It Computed?

Every state, including the District of Columbia, offers jobless
insurance programs that must conform to rules set down by federal law.

The states count all first-time filers for a given week ending on
Saturday and then transmit the data to the Labor Department in
Washington, which releases the figures to the public the following
Thursday.

Information on “insured unemployment”—that is, the total number of
unemployed currently receiving benefits—is published with a two-week
lag.

#### The Tables: Clues on What’s Ahead for the Economy

The initial unemployment claims report has shown an ability to predict
when the economy approaches a turning point. For instance, first-time
claims can hit their peak two to three months before the economy finally
bottoms out in recession and begins its recovery phase.

<span id="ch03a.html_ch03atab12"></span>Table. Unemployment Insurance
Data for Regular State Programs

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/03sei13.jpg)

</div>

\(1\) This is the number of new claims filed for unemployment insurance
benefits during the most recent week covered. A general rule of thumb is
that when first-time claims stand above 400,000 for several weeks, it’s
symptomatic of an economy that’s losing steam and in danger of slipping
into recession. Such a pace also drives the official unemployment rate
higher. On the flip side, a number that’s persistently below 375,000
suggests that a recovery is under way and companies are laying off fewer
workers. In addition, for the establishment survey to show any
meaningful jump in payroll employment, first-time claims must remain
below 325,000.

<span id="ch03a.html_page_57"></span>(2) Do not use a single week’s data
on initial claims to interpret a trend. The weekly series can be quite
erratic. Weeks containing holidays can easily distort the data on
filings. A four-day workweek, for example, can reduce claims by as much
as 20,000, only to have them surge the following week because they now
include those who didn’t have a chance to apply before. The solution is
to look at initial claims based on a four-week moving average, which is
reported here. The four-week average smooths out the volatility of the
weekly numbers.

\(3\) Another big issue for economists and politicians is whether the
total number of persons collecting unemployment insurance has been
increasing or decreasing over time. A figure of 3 million to 3.5 million
and climbing indicates a malfunctioning economy. Consumer confidence
suffers in such an environment, as does business investment. Economists
also wonder what effect all these benefit payments will have on federal
and state budgets. Perhaps the gravest concern, though, involves those
who lost their jobs and are ineligible to receive unemployment aid for
one reason or another. Jobless workers collecting unemployment insurance
at least have some funds to spend, which can soften the harmful effects
of an economic downturn. However, if total unemployment climbs (in the
household survey) at a faster rate than those collecting unemployment
insurance, it means a growing proportion of people out of work may have
to get by without any state financial support, and that could lead to
serious social dislocations. Without the safety net of benefit payments,
many turn to the underground economy or even to crime for money.

\(4\) The “insured unemployment rate” is another statistic worth
mentioning, albeit briefly. It’s the proportion of those currently
collecting unemployment insurance compared with the total number of
American workers who would be eligible to receive these benefits.
Although the investment community mostly ignores this figure, a few
economists follow its performance so that they can compare it with the
official unemployment rate in the household data.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_58"></span>Market Impact

##### Bonds

The fixed-income market reacts favorably when the number of new filings
for unemployment insurance picks up, especially if it jumps by more than
30,000 applications. A rise in first-time claims points to a weaker
economy and diminishing inflation pressures. What unnerves bond
investors is a continuous drop in claims, because it hints at a sturdier
economic climate ahead. That can prompt fresh concerns about future
inflation and lead to lower bond prices and rising yields.

##### Stocks

Equities tend to fare badly when there’s a persistent increase in
jobless claims. Though such a report would lower interest rates, which
is normally a positive for stocks, evidence of a serious deterioration
in the labor market augurs poorly for the economy, corporate profits,
and share prices.

##### Dollar

Falling interest rates make the dollar less attractive to hold,
especially if yields are higher in other countries. Thus, a steady climb
in initial claims that stems from a languishing domestic economy might
turn foreign investors away from U.S. securities and thereby weaken the
dollar’s value in foreign exchange markets.

### <span id="ch03a.html_page_59"></span>Help-Wanted Online Advertising

**Market Sensitivity:** Low.

**What Is It:** A measure of job openings posted on the Internet.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.conference-board.org/data/helpwantedonline.cfm](http://www.conference-board.org/data/helpwantedonline.cfm)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.conference-board.org](http://www.conference-board.org)*

**Release Time:** 10:00 a.m. (ET); released around the 1st of each month
and covers the previous month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** The Conference Board.

**Revisions:** Revisions are done annually, usually in January.

#### Why Is It Important?

Why track help-wanted ads? It turns out to be a reasonable predictor of
the economy’s direction. When the number of these ads increases, it
signifies growing confidence in the business community about upcoming
sales and profits. The brighter the outlook, the more likely employers
will accelerate hiring. Should the number of ads for jobs shrink, it is
an indication that companies are getting nervous about the future.
Concerns that business might turn sour in the months ahead will cause
firms to postpone or cancel hiring plans.

The Conference Board, a New York business research group, has been
tallying job advertisements since the Truman Administration (1951), and
for many decades that metric was the only leading indicator of labor
demand in the economy. Month after month for more than half a century,
the organization counted classified job ads in leading newspapers from
around the country. It then computed a monthly index based on the volume
of such ads.

However, by the early 2000s that method became less effective as a labor
forecasting tool. That’s because the number of jobs posted in newspapers
declined as firms turned increasingly to the Internet to fill job
openings. The Web proved to be a less costly and more efficient way to
find new, qualified workers. By 2005, help-wanted ads online became the
most common way job seekers found employment and the preferred method by
firms to publish job openings. That same year the Conference Board began
to publish its monthly Help-Wanted Online reports. Three years later,
the research group ceased publishing its monthly count from print ads,
and replaced it with an expanded and more comprehensive Help-Wanted
Online series.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_60"></span>How Is It Computed?

The Conference Board, in conjunction with the data collecting firm of
Wanted Technology, counts online ads from more than 1,200 job boards in
the U.S. They include both newspaper-placed Internet ads and job
openings posted on online boards. The task of counting such ads is
complicated by the fact that the same posting might appear on numerous
Web sites. So every effort is made is to remove duplicate ads in order
to get a more precise measure of current labor demand.

The methodology used by the business research group is fairly
straightforward. All job ads are given the same weight regardless of
whether each listing seeks one employee or several, part-time or
full-time, a CEO or a minimum-wage fast-food worker. What is especially
noteworthy is the timing of when these counts take place. The
Help-Wanted Online survey computes the posted ads from the middle of one
month to the middle of the next month, which is the same survey period
conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics when it prepares the
market-sensitive monthly employment report. The Conference Board then
breaks down the data into great detail, dividing them by location
(national region, state, and major metropolitan cities) and even
occupation. Another important distinction they make is to highlight how
many of the total ads counted have appeared for the first time that
month. By tracking changes in the volume of new ads posted, we can draw
some conclusions about the state of the overall economy and its ability
to generate jobs.

Unlike the original series of help-wanted ads in newspapers, which
culminated in an index number for the month, the Help-Wanted Online
series looks at the full universe of online job vacancies and releases a
total count each month. This is a far superior approach because it
avoids sampling errors that can mar the quality of other statistical
surveys. Finally, the Conference Board applies seasonal adjustment
factors to the counts to permit more meaningful analysis.

#### The Tables: Clues on What’s Ahead for the Economy

Although this series is relatively new and needs to be observed over
several business cycles to determine its predictive value, the online
job count already shows promise as a sensitive leading indicator of
economic and employment trends. After all, you would expect help-wanted
ads to peak before an economy enters recession, since employers shut
down hiring fairly quickly if they suspect a softening business climate
ahead. That is precisely what we have seen so far with the Help-Wanted
Online ads. According to the Conference Board’s historical data
(available on its Web site), the number of both new and total online
help-wanted ads peaked eight months prior to the 2008–09 recession, and
<span id="ch03a.html_page_61"></span>ten months before the Bureau of
Labor Statistics’ payroll series turned south. This metric thus has the
potential to warn investors well in advance that labor-market conditions
are deteriorating, a precursor to an economy that is struggling.

Can this indicator also predict the end of a recession? No. Companies do
not rush to post job advertisements the instant economic activity revs
up. Instead, they first seek to push existing employees to work longer
hours in the early stages of a recovery. Beyond that, many firms will
try to rehire those who were initially laid off, since the former
employees are familiar with the work and require little new training.
Companies will ramp up new hires if the outlook for business sales
justifies that investment.

Nevertheless, one trend that has been observed going back even to the
days of job-wanted ads in newspapers is that once the listings increase,
it is followed about three to six months later with an upturn in hiring.
The reason is that it takes a while for people to respond to such
advertisements, be interviewed, have their credentials checked, and
finally get hired. Thus, the job-ads count, both total and new, can
serve as a leading indicator of payroll growth (from the establishment
survey), which the financial markets watch very closely.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_62"></span><span id="ch03a.html_page_63"></span>Market Impact

##### Bonds

There has not been much reaction to the release of this measure so far.
But that could easily change as evidence builds that it can serve as a
reliable leading indicator of changes in labor market conditions and of
economic activity. What also makes this metric attractive is its
timeliness; it is typically released at the end of the reported month.

##### Stocks

For reasons stated above, the equity market has yet to respond to the
Help-Wanted Online series. But analysts can extract valuable clues about
specific industries that appear to be doing well enough to seek out more
workers.

##### Dollar

This report has virtually no impact on the foreign exchange markets.

### <span id="ch03a.html_page_64"></span>Corporate Layoff and Hiring Announcements

**Market Sensitivity:** Low.

**What Is It:** Counts the number of planned job cuts and hirings
announced by public companies.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.challengergray.com/press/press.aspx](http://www.challengergray.com/press/press.aspx)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.challengergray.com](http://www.challengergray.com)*

**Release Time:** 7:30 a.m. (ET); published the first week after the end
of the reference month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

**Revisions:** No revisions are made to previously released data.

#### Why Is It Important?

Since the 1980s, there has been a continuous wave of mergers, plant
closings, restructurings, and consolidations. Such corporate changes are
to be expected in an open, competitive, and dynamic economy. But one
very painful byproduct of all this activity has been massive layoffs.
Displaced workers now must spend weeks and months, sometimes even
longer, trying to find new jobs. The resulting loss of income can
devastate the financial health of households and sharply curtail
consumer spending. Even those still clinging to their jobs tend to grow
uneasy as they wonder about their own security. Such widespread
uncertainty and stress can put consumers in a very sour mood, and if
this mood is felt on a large enough scale, layoffs can even drag an
economy into recession.

Of course, corporate plans to shrink payrolls tell only part of the job
market story. For at the same time, there are also companies that want
to expand their operations and are ready to ramp up hiring. It is this
incessant churning of jobs that makes the U.S. economy so resilient and
provides money managers with investment opportunities. After all, by
tracking which specific sectors are laying off workers and which are
actively employing, investors can better identify areas of strength and
weakness in the business community. But who has the time to collect
corporate announcements on jobs? Fortunately, there is a firm that not
only compiles such statistics each month but also makes them available
to the public on a timely basis.

Challenger, Gray & Christmas (CGC), an outplacement firm based in
Chicago, scans public information records for announcements on corporate
layoffs and hiring. The firm compiles the numbers, then breaks them down
by industry and geography, and even cites the reasons behind the latest
corporate announcements. (For instance, were jobs eliminated because of
outsourcing, bankruptcy, cost cutting, labor disputes, or some other
cause?) By organizing the statistics in this manner, the report can help
clarify those sectors in the economy that appear to be growing and those
possibly facing financial stress.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_65"></span>How Is It Computed?

CGC culls a variety of sources for announced layoffs and employment
plans, including press releases, newspapers, SEC filings, and trade
papers, and then adds them up. Both publicly traded and private firms
are included in the search. The firm begins a new count at the start of
each month and continues until three days or so before the end of that
month.

#### The Tables: Clues on What’s Ahead for the Economy

The value of this report is that it provides both a macro and a micro
picture of the single most important report card on the economy—the
performance of the job market. However, one has to be careful in
interpreting the data presented in this release. What might seem
intuitive at first could turn out to be misleading. For example, layoff
announcements cannot be utilized as a leading indicator of turning
points in the economy. That’s because since the 1980s, job-elimination
programs have become a permanent part of the American business landscape
and layoffs now occur in significant numbers at every stage of the
business cycle. Just look at the last two decades: Not only did we see
companies shed workers during the recession of the early 1990s, but we
also saw them continue to slash payrolls during the powerful growth
years later that decade. Indeed, between 2004 and 2006, when the economy
averaged more than 3% growth a year, layoffs actually accelerated to
*twice* the pace of the 1990s.

Nor is the Challenger data meant to correlate with the government’s own
monthly report on employment, or weekly claims for unemployment
benefits. The reason is that announced job eliminations are usually not
carried out in a matter of weeks, but are spread out over many months or
even years, and often through attrition or early retirement. Moreover,
should the economy bounce back during that time, some of these announced
layoffs might not happen at all. Finally, the geographical regions
listed in the Challenger report are based mostly on the location of the
company’s headquarters, yet many of these layoffs and hirings can take
place elsewhere, even outside the U.S.

Having said all that, this report does provide some useful clues for
investors. It tells which industries are doing well enough to add to
their payrolls, and point to those that are forced to proceed with
layoffs. A second distinction is that while most economic indicators
look back at what happened in previous months, the CGC release tends to
be more forward-looking because it reflects a company’s future plans.

Obviously, if a consistent pattern emerges across these job-related

<span id="ch03a.html_page_67"></span>weakening economy, whereas the

force firms to reduce other operating expenses, such as labor. This
chart lays out 24 possible explanations for why firms were forced to

One of the newer statistics in this report covers the hiring plans
announced by companies each month, information that can guide money
managers toward sectors that are growing. Another reason this data is
noteworthy is that there are few other sources that organize corporate
hiring plans the way CGC does. Companies are under no obligation to make
pronouncements if they want to employ more people.
<span id="ch03a.html_page_68"></span>However, they are required to do so
in the event of large workforce reductions. Firms with 100 employees or
more are mandated by federal regulations (the Worker Adjustment and
Retraining Notification Act, or WARN) to announce mass layoffs two
months in advance.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_69"></span>Market Impact

There was a time when investors barely took notice of the Challenger
report. That is changing. It is being studied with greater interest by
money managers and the business media. The change is due to two factors.
First, investors have become much more sensitive to any forward-looking
indicator on the labor market. The data inside may be based on previous
corporate announcements, but by aggregating upcoming layoffs and
hirings, this release adds another perspective on where the job market
is headed. Second, the report contains a lot more information now than
it had a decade or two ago, and this makes it more useful. Indeed, the
report was not even made available on its Web site for public viewing a
few years ago. It now is online and this gives everyone an opportunity
to view and analyze the data.

##### Bonds

For more than a decade, layoffs have taken place in significant numbers
without regard for the business cycle, so it is unlikely that
fixed-income investors will actively trade on this report. However, a
large and unexpected jump in layoffs that accompanies other economic
indicators showing economic weakness can serve as a bullish sign for the
bond market.

If the Challenger report noted a large upturn in hiring plans, it would
unnerve fixed-income investors. But they would probably wait for the
government’s main employment report, which is released a few days later,
before taking action.

##### Stocks

While equity investors do not react much to this report, it can be used
as an important research tool to assess which sectors and companies are
flourishing, and identify those that are compelled to shed workers.

##### Dollar

This report has no impact on the foreign exchange markets.

### <span id="ch03a.html_page_70"></span>Mass Layoff Statistics (MLS)

**Market Sensitivity:** Low.

**What Is It:** Measures actual layoffs in business and government.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.bls.gov/mls](http://www.bls.gov/mls)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.bls.gov](http://www.bls.gov)*

**Release Time:** 10:00 a.m. (ET); this report is out four weeks after
the end of the month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor.

**Revisions:** There are no revisions in the monthly report. However,
the BLS does update its seasonal adjustment factors annually, usually
with the January release, and then amends the data for the last five
years.

#### Why Is It Important?

There are presently two major sources of information on layoffs. One is
the Challenger, Gray & Christmas survey, which was discussed in the
preceding section (“[Corporate Layoff and Hiring
Announcements](#ch03a.html_ch03alev1sec5)”). Its data, however, covers
only announced corporate layoffs; it doesn’t follow up to see whether
these job-elimination plans were fully carried out. Yet companies have
been known to reduce or even cancel publicized job cuts once business
improves. A more useful metric might be one that tallies layoffs that
actually occurred! To locate data on actual layoffs, you have to turn to
the government’s Bureau of Labor Statistics, which releases a monthly
report appropriately titled “[Mass Layoff Statistics
(MLS)](#ch03a.html_ch03alev1sec6).” Though this indicator is not widely
known to investors and economic researchers, it contains information
that can have a direct bearing on future household spending and economic
growth.

The MLS report tracks “mass layoff events.” An “event” is defined as
each time a company or a government agency lays off 50 or more workers
at a single location within a five-week period. (For example, if GM lets
go 70 workers in its Detroit auto plant and another 100 at a second GM
plant in Ohio, and American Airlines in Chicago cuts its payroll by 200,
all in the same workweek, the BLS counts them as three “events”
involving 370 jobs.) The agency totals all mass layoff events each
month, along with the number of jobless workers who filed for
unemployment insurance as a result of those job cuts. In addition, the
agency categorizes layoffs by their duration (30 days or less out of
work versus 31 days or more). It then breaks down all the data by
industry and geographic location. There’s a lot of information here that
can be of value to investors and business leaders who want to track the
magnitude of actual layoffs, see which industries and regions in the
U.S. are ailing, and find out where there may be a surplus of skilled,
but unemployed, workers.

#### <span id="ch03a.html_page_71"></span>How Is It Computed?

The BLS first contacts state agencies for the latest initial
unemployment insurance claims. It then sorts through the data to find
out how many of those who filed a claim were the result of mass layoffs.
Companies and government agencies are also contacted to see how many of
the job eliminations lasted 31 days or longer. After compiling the
numbers, the BLS publishes two reports. One is the monthly “[Mass Layoff
Statistics](#ch03a.html_ch03alev1sec6),” which is what this section is
about, and the other is a quarterly release known as the “Extended Mass
Layoffs” report. The latter deals with employees who have been separated
from their jobs for more than a month. (This report is released
quarterly and published on the same Web site.)

#### The Tables: Clues on What’s Ahead for the Economy

During the past 20 years, job cutbacks involving large numbers have
occurred at virtually every stage of the business cycle, thus
diminishing the value of layoff reports as a forecasting tool.
Nevertheless, while it lacks use as a leading indicator, the MLS report
has other valuable information that cannot be found elsewhere.

<span id="ch03a.html_ch03atab18"></span>Table 1. Mass Layoff Events and
Initial Claimants for Unemployment Insurance

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/03sei19.jpg)

</div>

\(1\) The Events column tells you how many instances there were of mass
layoffs in the month. Each instance is defined as a single action that
led to the elimination of at least 50 employees during a five-week
period, regardless of the duration of their separation.

\(2\) Here’s where you’ll find the monthly totals for the number of
persons who put in claims for unemployment insurance as a direct result
of those event-triggered layoffs. This column might look puzzling at
first, because monthly totals for initial claims for unemployment
benefits appear way below what you would expect, given the higher number
of people filing for jobless benefits each week (see the section
“[Weekly Claims for Unemployment
Insurance](#ch03a.html_ch03alev1sec3)”). The reason for this is that
only 10% of all first-time claims for benefits are the result of mass
layoff events involving at least 50 people within a five-week period.
Most layoffs that lead to unemployment claims represent numbers that are
less than 50 persons per incident.

\(3\) The far-left column, labeled “Total,” combines mass layoff
activity in both the private and government sectors. To get a more
accurate sense of job losses in the private business community, it’s
necessary to view “Private non-farm.” Within that category falls
manufacturing, which is highly sensitive to changes in the business
cycle. Should mass layoff events in manufacturing turn substantially
higher, it can corroborate other economic evidence that business
activity is slowing and that factories are under pressure to slash
payrolls.

</div>

This table, which is only partially shown here, tells how widespread
