funds into the economy to make borrowing even cheaper. Should the
economy respond and start to turn up, the combination of very low yields
on short-term Treasuries and a rebound in yields on 10- and 30-year
bonds can produce a steep yield curve. It is symptomatic of an economy
moving from recession to growth again. After healthy growth resumes, the
Fed lifts short-term rates a little, and the yield curve returns to its
more normal spread of about 2.5 percentage points.

Clearly, the yield curve has had an enviable track record of predicting
turning points in the economy. But there are many other factors that can
affect the shape of the yield curve too. Countries such as China, Japan,
OPEC, and South Korea, which depend on exports for much of their
economic growth, will take the surplus dollars they earn from their
sales to the U.S. and buy Treasuries too. Such purchases enable these
countries to better manage the value of their own currencies in foreign
exchange markets. These countries do not want to have an overly strong
currency because that can harm their exports. To keep their currency
from significantly appreciating, they will buy more U.S. government
securities since that lifts the dollar’s value.

Does this mean the yield curve has permanently lost its relevance?
Absolutely not. Much depends on the *magnitude* of the inverted yield
curve and its duration—not simply because it happens to be nominally
inverted. One report by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis calculated
the probabilities of a recession based on the yield curve as follows: If
the curve is normal so that the 10-year Treasury bond yield is more than
1.2 percentage points above the three-month bill, the chance of
recession is less than 5%. When the yield
<span id="ch03e.html_page_354"></span>curve flattens and the two have
essentially the same yield, the probability of recession rises to 25%.
If the curve ends up inverted such that the yield on 3-month bills
stands 2.4 percentage points *above* the 10-year bond, the odds leap to
90% that an economic downturn will materialize within the next 18
months.

#### Market Impact

##### Bonds

Expectations of future growth and inflation by fixed-income traders
determine which Treasury debt maturities are the most attractive to buy.
Such preferences help shape the yield curve. However, since the outlook
for economic activity and price behavior can change, the yield curve is
constantly in a state of motion.

##### Stocks

The equity market has not taken the yield curve seriously in the past,
despite its proven forecasting record. This is surprising because stock
prices are based on expectations of future corporate earnings and
overall business activity, both of which can be foreseen by the behavior
of the yield curve. Indeed, studies have shown that the yield curve can
serve as an effective market-timing strategy, yet it remains
underappreciated among portfolio managers.

##### Dollar

Foreign-investor reaction to a flat or inverted yield curve is difficult
to predict. Much depends on the magnitude of the inverted yield curve,
which is how much higher short-term rates are above long-term rates, and
how U.S. short-term rates stack up against those of other countries. It
is possible that active foreign traders might choose to avoid investing
in the U.S. because a flat or inverted yield curve is a harbinger of
anemic growth, if not recession. That will cause the dollar to
depreciate in foreign exchange markets. However, if the yield curve is
so inverted that U.S. short-term rates are markedly higher than those of
other nations, it can attract an influx of “hot money” from overseas as
foreign investors seek to take advantage of the greater returns they can
receive here. What do we mean by “hot money”? It’s fast-moving money
from investors around the world who are constantly on the hunt for the
highest possible short-term gains. The instant an investment loses its
appeal (for example, when U.S. yields fall relative to their foreign
counterparts), that hot money quickly leaves the borders of one country
for another lucrative region of the world. Thus, the dollar might bounce
up in value when there is an inverted yield curve, but its strength
would be very tenuous.

A steep yield curves suggests stronger economic growth and rising
short-term rates in the months ahead. This will likely attract foreign
investors to purchase and hold dollar-based financial assets.

<span id="ch03f.html"></span>

### <span id="ch03f.html_page_355"></span><span id="ch03f.html_ch03f"></span>Other Noteworthy U.S. Economic Indicators: Credit Manager’s Index

**What Is It:** A report that evaluates credit conditions in the
business sector.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*<http://web.nacm.org/cmi/cmi.asp>*

**Release Time:** 9:00 a.m. (ET); released the last business day of the
month and covers conditions in that month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** National Association of Credit Management (NACM).

It is often said that credit is the lifeblood of an economy. Consumers
certainly use it extensively when they go shopping. But it’s also true
that companies rely on credit when they purchase equipment, supplies,
and inventories. Sellers of these goods are willing to extend credit to
their business customers so that they will come back and buy more. When
the economy is growing, these customers typically increase purchases,
often on credit, and they tend to make timely payments. But when
business conditions start to sour, firms that financed their purchases
might find it more difficult to come up with the funds to make their
scheduled payments. This begins to raise some red flags on the health of
the economy and should be a concern to investors and business leaders.
One way to keep an eye on such trends is to follow the Credit Manager’s
Index.

Every month the National Association of Credit Management, a trade group
of credit managers and collection professionals, surveys members to see
whether credit conditions are improving or deteriorating. The index
focuses on credit conditions at the business-to-business level and is
based on answers to some key questions: Have credit managers observed
that their corporate customers are having a tougher time meeting their
financial obligations? Have disputes with creditors increased? Are more
companies seeking bankruptcy protection from creditors? Are applications
for credit increasing or decreasing?

A material change in business credit conditions can be a fairly good
leading indicator of economic turning points, and for that reason this
metric has attracted more interest among professional forecasters and
investors.

### <span id="ch03f.html_page_356"></span>Small Business Economic Trends

**What Is It:** An important report that tells us how confident small
companies are about the economy, and how that will affect their own
future business plans.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.nfib.com/research-foundation/surveys/small-business-economic-trends](http://www.nfib.com/research-foundation/surveys/small-business-economic-trends)*

**Release Time:** 7:30 a.m. (ET); released the second Tuesday of each
month and contains observations made during the previous month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB).

Anyone who ignores this survey does so at great peril. Small businesses
are the most dynamic part of the U.S. economy—so much so that they
create two out of every three new jobs. Small businesses are also the
first to ramp up production and hire workers as an economy emerges from
recession, and the first to shut down factories and dismiss workers when
business activity weakens. This tendency to react quickly and adroitly
to the changing economic climate is why it’s important to know what the
small-business community thinks about the economic outlook. These
expectations can greatly influence trends in employment and capital
spending.

Fortunately, the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB)
releases a monthly survey that takes the pulse of this business group.
Among the most closely watched measures in this report is a table called
the Small Business Optimism Index. It summarizes what executives think
about future business conditions and why. What follows next, however, is
just as crucial. Based on their answers to key questions, we get to see
what actions these firms say they are inclined to take in the coming
months: Is it a good time to expand? What plans do they have about
pricing? Are they going to accelerate hiring? Will they buy more
inventories in the coming months? Are they going to increase capital
expenditures? The survey even asks small-business owners to identify the
single biggest problem they face. The NFIB, which has more than 350,000
members, began its survey as a quarterly report back in 1973. But as
interest grew in getting more timely data from this important sector, it
began to conduct a monthly poll, starting in 1986.

### <span id="ch03f.html_page_357"></span>Cass Freight Index

**What Is It:** A report that assesses the monthly volume and
transportation costs of freight moving across North America.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.cassinfo.com/frtindex.html](http://www.cassinfo.com/frtindex.html)*

**Release Time:** No specific time of day; released in the first week of
every month and covers shipping activity during the preceding month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Cass Information Systems, Inc.

At the very core of a functioning modern economy is the efficiency of
its supply-chain network. When we say “supply chain,” we are talking in
large part about a nationwide transportation system (trucks, planes, and
railroad cars) that carries critical commodities and finished goods to a
variety of destinations that include ports, factories, wholesalers, and
retailers across North America. Monitoring the ebb and flows of traffic
in the supply-chain network can tell us a great deal about how the
economy is performing. Two major indicators that do this very well are
the monthly Cass Freight Index and the Weekly Railroad Traffic report,
which is covered in the next section.

The Cass Freight Index actually consists of two measures. The first
reflects the volume of products that are shipped in a particular month.
As you can imagine, when an economy gathers more steam, factories
increase orders for basic materials so that they can speed up
production. Retailers will ask suppliers to deliver more inventories to
satisfy rising consumer demand. Manufacturers are also shipping greater
volumes of goods to key U.S. ports for loading on merchant ships
destined to fast-growing emerging countries. A strong U.S. and
international economy will have the entire supply-chain network busy
transporting items to where they are needed. On the other hand, a
weakening global economy will do the reverse, with the volume of
shipments diminishing.

The second measure tracked by Cass Freight Index reflects changes in the
cost of shipping. Obviously, numerous factors can influence
expenditures—the cost of fuel, shortages of shipping capacity, and the
competition for qualified drivers, which can drive up wages. All these
factors can have an inflationary impact on the U.S. economy, especially
at the producer price level. The report itself is put together by Cass
Information Systems, which processes more than \$20 billion in freight
transactions annually on behalf of 350 large shippers. Both the freight
volume and the expenditure data are derived directly from these
operations.

### <span id="ch03f.html_page_358"></span>Weekly Railroad Traffic (Freight)

**What Is It:** A timely report on the volume and types of commodities
carried by rail freight cars across the country.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.aar.org/NewsAndEvents/Freight-Rail-Traffic.aspx](http://www.aar.org/NewsAndEvents/Freight-Rail-Traffic.aspx)*

**Release Time:** Between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. (ET); released every
Thursday and covers freight rail traffic in the preceding week.

**Frequency:** Weekly.

**Source:** Association of American Railroads.

Very few economic reports possess the qualities of being both
exceptionally timely and sensitive to shifts in the business cycle. One
that does have such attributes is the weekly report on freight traffic
in North America by the Association of American Railroads (AAR). This
release, formally called Weekly Railroad Traffic, contains separate
tables on freight rail traffic in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico and is
based on reporting by 13 major railroads. The data is presented in a
well-organized format. First, it looks at traffic in terms of carloads,
which can be in boxcars, hoppers, or tank cars, and they often carry raw
or intermediate-level commodities. These goods generally make their way
to factories. The AAR tracks some 20 different commodities that these
carloads transport, including lumber, petroleum products, coal,
chemicals, and metals. An economy on the rebound will increase demand
for these items, and that shows up in the number of freight cars
carrying such commodities during the preceding week.

The report also monitors rail traffic of intermodal units. Intermodals
are structures physically placed on rail cars that can be carried on
different modes of transportation. For instance, a flatbed rail car can
carry a trailer (with wheels) that eventually gets hooked to a truck at
a final destination. Another intermodal unit is an enclosed container
(which has no wheels) that is lifted off a rail car and moved onto
either a cargo ship or a flatbed truck. Intermodal units generally
contain finished goods and get delivered to warehouses or retail stores.
Both carloads and intermodal units move in tandem with the business
cycle. However, some commodities carried on carloads—such as lumber or
chemicals—can serve as leading indicators of economic activity, which is
why the Weekly Railroad Traffic reports can be useful in understanding
where the economy stands in the business cycle.

### <span id="ch03f.html_page_359"></span>Architecture Billings Index

**What Is It:** The index measures demand for architectural services and
can foreshadow commercial construction activity.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.aia.org/practicing/economics/](http://www.aia.org/practicing/economics/)*

**Release Time:** 8:30–9:00 a.m. (ET); released the third or fourth
Wednesday of each month and covers activity in the preceding month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** American Institute of Architects.

One of the largest sectors in the U.S. economy is commercial
construction. This \$800 billion industry accounts for about 5% of GDP
and employs millions of workers. It is also an excellent barometer of
overall confidence in the U.S. economy. Indeed, when the economy is on a
sustained growth path, spending on commercial construction typically
accelerates faster than most other sectors. But then when doubts arise
about the economic outlook, few sectors fall faster. Given the planning
and capital costs involved in nonresidential construction, confidence in
the economic outlook is an essential prerequisite for these projects to
proceed. To help fellow architects better assess the climate for
commercial construction activity, the American Institute of Architects
(AIA) in 1995 began to poll a number of architecture firms for the
latest trends in billing for services. Today, some 300 architecture
companies participate in a monthly survey to report whether billings
have increased, decreased, or remained the same in the preceding month.
The AIA then computes a diffusion index in which a score of more than 50
indicates that most firms are seeing an increase in activity, whereas a
score below 50 means that respondents have seen a decline in business.

One reason the Architecture Billings Index has grown in popularity among
forecasters is that an increase in billings can foreshadow a pickup in
construction activity within the next 9 to 12 months. A construction
boom will not only benefit architects but also increase the demand for
construction material, equipment, and labor, all of which help fuel more
economic activity.

### <span id="ch03f.html_page_360"></span>S&P/Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index

**What Is It:** Many people believe this series is the most reliable in
calculating changes in the price of single-family homes.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.homeprice.standardandpoors.com](http://www.homeprice.standardandpoors.com)*

**Release Time:** 9:00 a.m. (ET); released the last Tuesday of each
month and contains home price changes of two months earlier.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Standard & Poor’s, Fiserv, and MacroMarkets LLC.

Although there are a dozen or so indicators that track changes in home
prices around the country, many analysts point to the S&P/Case-Shiller
series as perhaps the most accurate of the bunch. Two economics
professors and a private money manager—Robert Shiller of Yale, Karl Case
at Wellesley, and Allen Weiss—collaborated in the 1980s and 1990s to
come up with a more precise calculation of how much home prices change
over time. Shiller, in particular, has earned a well-deserved reputation
for being far ahead of the curve in spotting dangerous excesses in the
valuation of assets, particularly in real estate and stock prices. The
S&P/Case-Shiller Home Price Index represents a continuation of the
excellent research he and his colleagues have done. What makes this
series stand out is that it tracks only homes that sold at least twice
during a covered period. By following price changes for the same
single-family home over time, one can get a more reliable measure of how
real estate values change. In contrast, prices published by the Commerce
Department and by Realtors can be skewed because they can include a
different mix of homes sold each month.

Case-Shiller indexes are calculated monthly, and are based on a
three-month moving average. For example, January’s data will be shaped
by sales that have also taken place in November and December. Keep in
mind that Case-Shiller does not report prices by giving a dollar figure.
Instead, an index is compiled from which percent changes are calculated
to show how prices have moved from the preceding month and from a
year-ago level. The year-over-year figure is judged to be more
meaningful. Its two most popular metropolitan groupings are the 10- and
20-city composite price indexes.

<span id="ch04.html"></span>

## <span id="ch04.html_page_361"></span>Chapter 4. International Economic Indicators: Why Are They So Important?

U.S. economic indicators help us understand what is happening in the
domestic economy. However, to be a successful investor or an effective
corporate leader in today’s highly integrated global economy also
requires knowledge of what is going on beyond U.S. borders. A CEO who
wants to sell products overseas or an investor who seeks to achieve
higher returns on stocks and bonds should be familiar with indicators
that gauge the health of foreign economies.

Why place so much emphasis on the international business climate? One
reason is that most of the growth in the world economy is taking place
within the emerging countries, not the large industrial nations.
Secondly, the performance of U.S. corporate profits, stocks and bonds,
and the dollar is affected by foreign developments more than ever
before. A recession in Europe harms not only companies on that
continent, but many U.S.-based firms as well. Close to half of the
earnings of S&P 500 firms originate from sales outside the U.S.
Companies in the energy and technology sectors, for example, generate
more than half of their revenues abroad. Moreover, it just makes good
business sense to be aware of new opportunities that become available in
markets outside the U.S. By diversifying into Europe, Asia, and Latin
America, one is no longer bound to the economic swings of just one
country. Indeed, there is much fertile territory to choose from in other
markets. Equity investors, for example, can pick from more than 45,000
public companies that are listed on world stock exchanges, 75% of which
are outside the U.S.

To be sure, there are additional risks to consider when investing
overseas. One of the biggest is adverse movements in currencies. If you
own securities or other assets in another country and their currency
climbs in value against the dollar, great! The overall return on that
investment gets an added lift because it is more valuable in dollar
terms. However, should that currency happen to weaken relative to the
dollar, the investment will be less valuable or perhaps even turn into a
loss when it is sold and the proceeds are converted back to dollars.
Thus, shifts in foreign exchange values can potentially make or break a
foreign investment.

<span id="ch04.html_page_362"></span>Given the risks currencies pose,
wouldn’t it make more sense to simply shy away from international
markets? Absolutely not. There is nothing inherently mysterious about
the movement of the dollar, euro, yen, British pound, or any of the
other major free-floating currencies in the foreign exchange markets,
for ultimately, the long-term value of a currency is determined by a
country’s economic fundamentals. Is the economy growing? Does inflation
remain under control? Are consumers and businesses confident about the
future of their economy? Are government fiscal policies responsible?
Does the country have adequate savings for investments? Is its
international trade account in reasonable balance? These are the issues
that have the greatest influence in determining currency values. Sure,
exchange rates might fluctuate in the short term due to differences in
interest rates or from occasional uncertainties born of economic or
political instability. But, by and large, the true value of a currency
is based on the economic soundness and vitality of the country behind
it.

Another criticism heard about entering foreign markets is that the
benefits of global diversification have been oversold. According to this
argument, markets overseas increasingly appear to march in lock step
with those in the U.S., so why bother investing elsewhere, where the
risks are greater? It is true that during periods of crises, whether
they be economic, political, or military, markets around the world tend
to move in unison. However, such moments of high global tension are
uncommon, and these parallel movements in the value of assets around the
world are usually very brief—a matter of days or weeks at most.
Generally, foreign financial markets tend to pursue their own direction.
Canada’s stock market historically has a 65% correlation with the U.S.;
for the U.K. it is 50%. German equities have a 55% correlation, and
Japan has less than 20% relationship. Case in point: Just look at the
best and worst performers by national stock markets over the last
several years, as shown in [Table 4.1](#ch04.html_ch04tab01).

<span id="ch04.html_ch04tab01"></span>Table 4.1. Ranking Stock Market
Performance by Country (Based on Local Currencies)

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04tab01.jpg)

</div>

As you can see, the U.S. is listed just once among the top performers in
recent years. The point of this table is to underscore the importance of
keeping an open mind about
<span id="ch04.html_page_363"></span>investing in foreign markets,
especially in the emerging countries. While no one can predict with
certainty which economies and financial markets will outperform others,
one outcome is assured. Over the next generation we will see hundreds of
millions of new middle-class consumers emerge in the developing
countries, and they will be the main driving force in the global economy
for decades to come. There should thus be no dispute that the virtues of
diversifying investments abroad remain as valid as ever.

This chapter is designed to take you to the next level, which is to
identify the foreign indicators that provide the best read on current
and future global economic conditions. Certain barometers of economic
activity abroad should be followed with the same regularity and scrutiny
as U.S. indicators so that investors and business managers have a chance
of achieving success in international markets. The problem, much like
with the U.S., is that there is a vast amount of foreign economic data
in the public domain. Hundreds of countries churn out thousands of
statistics on a regular basis. Even if you narrowed down the number of
countries worth monitoring to two dozen, the task of following all the
indicators that flow from these nations can still be overwhelming.
Besides the sheer variety of international statistics, many of them are
difficult to locate when needed. Often they are defined and computed
differently than indicators in the U.S. and can vary greatly in quality.
A large number are not even presented in English.

This section tries to overcome these problems. In the following pages,
we select the most important foreign economic indicators for closer
study. They represent the three major non-U.S. markets in the world:
Europe, Asia, and Latin America. As is the case with U.S. economic
statistics, these foreign indicators are released to the public on a
predetermined schedule. Calendars of international economic releases can
be found on the Web sites listed at the start of [Chapter
6](#ch06.html_ch06), “[Best Web Sites for International Economic
Indicators](#ch06.html_ch06).” All the international indicators
presented here are available on the Internet. They originate from either
official government or private association Web sites, are free to the
public, and can be viewed in English.

Finally, note that international data is presented in different formats.
Many countries use commas instead of decimal points and a period or a
space instead of a comma to indicate the thousands place. For example,
the U.S. and Germany both represent numbers using decimal points and
commas, but sometimes the symbols are interchanged (2,325.77 versus
2.325,77). At other times, Germany (and France) might use a space as the
digit-grouping symbol (2 325,77).

International dates are also displayed differently around the world. In
the U.S., the month precedes the day; Europeans mostly use
day-month-year, whereas Asian cultures use year-month-day. Why isn’t
there a single standard for all countries now that world economic and
financial systems are so closely integrated? Tradition and politics.
These two hurdles are difficult to overcome. Those favoring a uniform
worldwide format will have a long wait. In the meantime, one has little
choice but to get used to these local customs and move on.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_364"></span>German Industrial Production

**What Is It:** Industrial output in Europe’s largest economy.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.destatis.de/EN/Homepage.html](http://www.destatis.de/EN/Homepage.html)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.destatis.de](http://www.destatis.de)*

**Release Time:** 11:00 a.m. (Continental time); released the first or
second week of the month and refers to activity two months earlier (so
March data describes production in January).

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Federal Statistics Office, Germany (Statistisches Bundesamt,
Deutschland).

**Revisions:** Revisions can occur with each release and cover the two
preceding months.

We begin with Germany, Europe’s richest and most populous country. Its
output alone accounts for a third of everything produced in the
Eurozone, the name given to the region of 17
countries<sup><a href="#ch04.html_ch04fn01a" id="ch04.html_ch04fn01">*</a></sup>
that use the euro currency. Germany thus holds enormous sway over the
Continent’s well being. It is the country all of Europe relies on to
help solve the region’s economic woes. However, Germany’s influence also
extends far beyond Europe. It is the world’s fifth-largest economy and
the second-biggest exporter. It is also a key trading partner of the
U.S. and an important investor. Trade between the two countries now
exceeds \$140 billion. Outside of Europe, the U.S. is Germany’s biggest
economic partner. Indeed, German companies account for about 800,000
jobs in the U.S., and American firms have established roughly 500,000
positions in Germany.

<a href="#ch04.html_ch04fn01" id="ch04.html_ch04fn01a">*</a> As of this
writing, 17 countries use the euro as their currency: Austria, Belgium,
Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy,
Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, and
Spain.

Given the dominance of its economy over Europe and the fact that it is a
key player in the world as well, Germany’s industrial production figure
ranks at the top of the must-watch list. Though industrial output
accounts for less than a quarter of the country’s GDP, this indicator
has been correlated with GDP changes in the Eurozone overall. Thus,
investors and business executives who want to spot early signs of
strength or weakness in Europe will find Germany’s industrial production
index a good leading indicator.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_365"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei01.jpg)

</div>

### <span id="ch04.html_page_366"></span>German IFO Business Climate Index

**What Is It:** German business leaders assess the current and future
economic climate.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.cesifo-group.de/portal/page/portal/ifoHome/a-winfo](http://www.cesifo-group.de/portal/page/portal/ifoHome/a-winfo)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.cesifo-group.de/portal/page/portal/ifoHome](http://www.cesifo-group.de/portal/page/portal/ifoHome)*

**Release Time:** 10:30 a.m. (Continental time); published the third or
fourth week of the survey month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** The CESifo Group.

**Revisions:** Tend to be rare. Periodic revisions occur as a result of
changes in seasonal adjustment factors.

Among the most anticipated economic statistics to come out in Europe
every month is Germany’s IFO Business Climate Index. From the time it
was launched in 1949, this series has proven to be a very good leading
indicator of how the German economy and, more broadly, the European
economy will perform in the weeks ahead. Of course, a similar claim was
made of the industrial production index. But what makes the IFO report
such a sensitive one for investors is the timeliness of the data—the
results are released the same month the survey is taken.

At the start of every month, the Institute questions more than 7,000
German business leaders and senior managers covering the manufacturing,
construction, wholesale, and retailing industries. All are asked to
appraise Germany’s current business situation (good/satisfactory/poor),
as well as their expectations over the next six months (more
favorable/unchanged/more unfavorable). Their answers form the basis of
the total Business Climate Index and its two principal subcomponents:
the Present Situations Index, which assesses current economic
conditions, and the Expectations Index, where those queried are asked to
forecast what the business environment might be a half year later.

Of the three index results, European financial markets tune in more
closely to the expectations series. History has shown that movements in
the Expectations Index tend to lead changes in the Eurozone’s industrial
production by about two or three months. Thus, if the IFO expectations
gauge turns up, odds are it will shortly be followed by an acceleration
in factory output in Germany and perhaps much of Europe as well.

After the reunification of Germany, the IFO Institute initially
published two separate business climate readings—one for eastern Germany
and the other for western Germany. However, in 2004, the decision was
made to combine the two sets of data to represent business activity in
Germany as a whole. Economists at the IFO believed that the business
cycles for these two regions had by now largely converged, even though
they were still <span id="ch04.html_page_367"></span>operating at
different output levels. Thus, the IFO Business Climate Index now
publishes a united German series for its headline index. Those who still
want to see separate performance data for western and eastern Germany
can do so by searching the more detailed IFO database on its Web sites.

Finally, it is interesting to note that the IFO Business Climate Index
appears to have a close correlation with the U.S.’s own Institute for
Supply Management (ISM) manufacturing report. Over the years, a
persistent rise in the ISM numbers has, after a six-month lag, been
accompanied by an increase in the German IFO expectations index. Given
the size and importance of the American economy in the world, this
probably is not all that surprising. This linkage between the two
surveys is yet another illustration of how interwoven the international
economy has become.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei02.jpg)

</div>

*Source:* IFO Institute for Economic Research, used with permission.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_368"></span>German Consumer Price Index (CPI)

**What Is It:** The main price inflation gauge for Europe’s largest
economy.

**News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.destatis.de](http://www.destatis.de)* (click “English”)

**Home Web Address:** *[www.destatis.de](http://www.destatis.de)*

**Release Time:** 7:00 a.m. (Continental time); the preliminary CPI is
published around the 25th of every month. Final figures are released two
weeks later.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Federal Statistics Office Germany (Statistisches Bundesamt
Deutschland).

**Revisions:** Monthly report on the CPI might contain revisions for
earlier months.

As the economic pillar of Europe, Germany can serve as the engine of
growth for the Continent, or it can be responsible for dragging down the
region. Which role Germany ultimately plays depends on many factors, but
none more important than the performance of its own inflation. Germany’s
CPI can have a powerful impact on the economies of other European
nations and on the policies of the European Central Bank (ECB), which
sets short-term interest rates for all 17 countries using the euro
currency.<sup><a href="#ch04.html_ch04fn02" id="ch04.html_ch04fn02a">*</a></sup>

<a href="#ch04.html_ch04fn02a" id="ch04.html_ch04fn02">*</a> See the
earlier section on German industrial production for the names of 17
countries sharing the euro.

If German inflation is increasing at a troubling rate, the ECB will
likely raise interest rates even if the other neighboring economies show
their inflation to be relatively tame. On the other extreme, should
Germany get caught up in a deflationary spiral in which prices are
consistently falling, the ECB is expected to jump in and lower rates to
preempt a similar collapse in prices from spreading to the rest of the
continent.

Germany’s CPI has been on the radar screen of investors worldwide for
decades. Its high profile can be traced to the country’s oath to avoid
at all costs a repetition of the catastrophic hyperinflation it
experienced in the 1920s, when prices for essentials like bread and milk
jumped several hundred percent every day, making its national currency
essentially worthless. That painful memory led the Bundesbank (Germany’s
central bank) after World War II to set in stone a tough, inflexible,
anti-inflationary policy, and it has never veered from that stance. For
decades the Bundesbank showed zero tolerance for the slightest whiff of
inflation beyond 2% a year. It made no difference whether the economy
was weak or unemployment was sky-high. The primary mandate of the
central bank was to keep inflation close to zero and protect Germany’s
currency, the deutsche mark, at all costs, even if it meant lifting and
holding rates at painfully high levels. Although Germany’s dogged
defense against inflation contributed to years of chronically high
joblessness, it also made its currency one of the most revered in the
world.

<span id="ch04.html_page_369"></span>During talks to establish the euro
in the 1990s, Germany made clear to European negotiators that it would
join the currency union only if the new European Central Bank agreed to
pursue the same tough anti-inflationary position shown by the
Bundesbank. German officials wanted the euro to have the kind of
respectability in global currency markets that the mark had. That would
mean keeping interest-rate decisions for Eurozone nations out of the
hands of politicians. Even today, Germany’s influence on the ECB is
palpable; Europe’s central bank firmly toes the line that it will not
permit inflation to exceed the 2% range for the Eurozone.

This does not mean the ECB as a matter of policy will disregard all
other economic stresses in the region. During the gravest moments of the
Eurozone’s sovereign debt crisis, for example, the central bank
surprised many by showing a more pragmatic side. As the danger of
sovereign defaults in Europe grew in 2011, many feared that the fallout
would ultimately lead to a catastrophic collapse of the Eurozone. But
the ECB boldly dropped short-term rates to a historic low and lent out
massive amounts of low-cost funds to nervous European banks—and did so
*even though* inflation in the region remained above the central bank’s
target.

Let’s take a closer look at Germany’s inflation measure itself. The CPI
measures the average change in prices for all goods and services bought
by households for the purpose of consumption. In the middle of the
month, about 560 price collectors, working out of state government
offices across Germany, collect prices on a basket of 750 specific goods
and services. Overall, approximately 400,000 prices are obtained each
month, including taxes (value-added and excise taxes) and price
discounts (such as sales or rebates). The Federal Statistics Office
(FSO) then compiles these price changes for six key German states
(Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Brandenburg, Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia,
and Saxony) and announces the much-awaited preliminary inflation rate
for the month, along with the latest 12-month change.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei03.jpg)

</div>

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei04.jpg)

</div>

Another virtue of the German CPI is how current it is. The government
puts out a provisional estimate of inflation around the third or fourth
week of the month. A final CPI is published two weeks later, between the
10th and 15th of the following month. It is the provisional figures,
though, that traders in the financial markets react to most because the
difference between the preliminary German CPI and the revised numbers
tends to be negligible.

Without meaning to complicate this subject, it is necessary to know that
the FSO also calculates another version of Germany’s inflation every
month, which is in the same press release. Why produce two CPI versions?
The reason for the second version is to follow a standardized European
formula for measuring the CPI. This allows business leaders, investors,
and economists to more accurately compare Germany’s inflation rates with
those of its neighboring countries. Called the Harmonized Index of
Consumer Prices (HICP), and dubbed “hiccup,” it is the official
inflation computation for the 27 member states of the European Union
(EU), plus Norway, Iceland, and Switzerland. When all is
<span id="ch04.html_page_370"></span>said and done, though, the
difference between the national definition of the German CPI and the
Harmonized CPI for Germany is not significant.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_371"></span>ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment

**What Is It:** A popular, near-real-time survey of confidence from top
investors in Germany.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.zew.de/en/publikationen/Konjunkturerwartungen/Konjunkturerwartungen.php3](http://www.zew.de/en/publikationen/Konjunkturerwartungen/Konjunkturerwartungen.php3)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.zew.de/en//index.php3](http://www.zew.de/en//index.php3)*

**Release Time:** 11:00 a.m. (local time); released midmonth and covers
survey results of the same month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** ZEW Centre for European Economic Research.

This final indicator from Germany came into being two decades ago and
has two impressive features going for it. First, the report is released
in the same month the survey covers, which makes it quite timely, and
second, it has a fairly impressive track record as a leading economic
indicator of the German economy. Here’s how it is designed. The ZEW
Centre for European Economic Research solicits responses from around 300
investors and analysts during the first two weeks of every month on what
they expect economic conditions in Germany will be in six months. More
specifically, they are asked about their outlook for inflation, short-
and medium-term interest rates, the yield on ten-year German government
bonds, stock market indexes, currencies, the profitability of firms, and
even forecasts on the price of oil.

But here’s one other aspect about this release that makes it so
worthwhile to follow. These financial experts are told to assess future
conditions not only in Germany, but also for the Eurozone, the United
States, Japan, Great Britain, France, and Italy. The questions are all
on a single page, which allows for faster processing of the responses
and a quicker turnaround time for the results to be released to the
public. Thus, each month we get a near-real-time appraisal from European
investors on where they see certain key world economies heading.

The calculation used to compute the index is quite direct. The index
represents the difference between the percentage share of analysts who
are optimistic and the share of analysts who are pessimistic. So if 55%
of participants expect the German economic situation to improve within
the next six months, 20% expect no change, and 25% expect the economic
situation to deteriorate, the ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment would
have an index value of plus 30. A positive number thus means that the
share of optimists outweighs the share of pessimists, and vice versa.

This report is closely followed by European investors and economists and
is known to be highly correlated with the IFO Business Climate Index
mentioned earlier. That makes it a major market-mover in Europe.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_372"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei05.jpg)

</div>

*Source:* ZEW Centre for European Economic Research, used with
permission.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_373"></span>Japan Industrial Production

**What Is It:** Measures the change in monthly industrial output.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.meti.go.jp/english/statistics](http://www.meti.go.jp/english/statistics)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.meti.go.jp/english](http://www.meti.go.jp/english)*

**Release Time:** 8:50 a.m. (local time); a preliminary report is
released in the final week of the next month. A revised report is
published another two to three weeks later. (For example, data on
October is announced during the last week in November, to be followed by
another report on revisions in mid-December.)

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI).

**Revisions:** Monthly and annual revisions are frequent and can be
substantial.

Few modern economies have faced as many predicaments as Japan. After
achieving one of the highest growth rates in the world from the 1960s to
the 1980s, Japan has since struggled to regain its footing. A severe
stock market and real estate crash brought repeated recessions in the
1990s, with many labeling those years as Japan’s lost decade. To get the
country back on its feet, Japan’s central bank lowered short-term rates
to near zero, and the government put through a series of financial and
regulatory reforms to encourage more borrowing, spending, and
investment. The results were encouraging. After several false starts
earlier this decade, the economy appeared to be on the mend. But then
came the devastating earthquake in 2011, which shook the nation to its
core. The violent movement of the earth unleashed a horrific tsunami and
brought the country close to a nuclear catastrophe with the meltdown of
its Fukushima reactor. While the economy will ultimately benefit from
the billions being poured in to rebuild the affected area, Japan’s woes
are far from over. It still faces an aging population, high public debt,
an excessive reliance on exports for economic growth, and has to rely on
imports to supply virtually all the fuel it needs.

Despite all these challenges, Japan’s importance to the international
economy and its influence in global capital markets remains largely
undiminished. It holds title as the biggest exporter of investment
capital in the world and owns an economy exceeded in size only by the
U.S. and China. It sells \$850 billion worth of goods and services a
year to other nations. Japanese companies are also powerful competitors
in several major industries, such as autos, electronics, and robotics.
Moreover, the yen continues to stand alongside the U.S. dollar and the
euro as one of the three most important currencies. For all these
reasons, global investors and business leaders, especially those in the
U.S., closely monitor Japan’s economic health.

Also looming large for Americans is the fact that Japan is the
second-largest foreign owner of U.S. Treasury securities. As a result,
Japanese banks, insurance companies, and
<span id="ch04.html_page_374"></span>government agencies have helped
fund the U.S. government budget for years, lending hundreds of billions
of dollars. However, this is also a cause for concern. Serious financial
and economic problems in Japan could easily spill over into the U.S.
Investors in Japan, for example, might decide to purchase less U.S.
Treasury debt or even sell some of their holdings in dollar-based
financial assets. They can also choose to manipulate the value of the
yen to help export sales. Indeed, few countries in the world intervene
in the currency markets as much as Japan.

Given the ability of Japan’s economy to affect asset values in world
capital markets and to sway currency markets, foreign investors know
they have to stay informed about the soundness of the economy. That
means paying particularly close attention to its industrial production,
which many experts consider to be one of the best barometers of business
activity in Japan. Analysts prefer to monitor industrial output over GDP
because the former comes out sooner, responds faster to changes in the
business climate, and is rich with information on the country’s
manufacturing and mining industries. In fact, Japan’s industrial
production release is more comprehensive in its coverage of the economy
than its U.S. counterpart. Case in point: Japan’s monthly production
report even includes forecasts of how key manufacturers are expected to
perform in the next two months.

In view of all the attention paid to Japanese manufacturers, it might be
surprising to learn that manufacturing activity makes up less than a
quarter of the GDP. But this figure is very misleading because the
actual impact that manufacturers have on the economy is much greater.
For example, exports represent a primary engine of growth for Japan.
Strong foreign demand for cars, digital cameras, HDTVs, and computer
accessories feeds right through to the domestic economy by stimulating
capital investment spending, employment, and overall output.

Japan started measuring industrial production in 1953, and it now
includes virtually all privately owned companies in mining and
manufacturing, regardless of size. The main task of the industrial
production series is to compute monthly changes in output for 536 items.
Figures are also given for the actual quantity of goods being produced,
shipped, and kept in inventory for many commodities.

The initial release, called the Preliminary Report on Indices of
Industrial Production, is published a month after the period being
covered ends. A revised release is issued about three weeks later. One
can access the industrial production report in two ways. There is a
summary report on the Web
([www.meti.go.jp/english/statistics/](http://www.meti.go.jp/english/statistics/)).
Inside that report is another link where you can download the complete
72-page release as a PDF file. The tables shown in this section come
from that detailed report. Data is presented in both English and
Japanese and is well organized, with years and dates on the right.
Figures are seasonally adjusted with an index base of 100 that is
currently tied to the year 2005. Keep in mind that revisions are
frequent and can be very large.

<span id="ch04.html_page_375"></span>• Mining and Manufacturing:
Industrial Production

\(1\) This is the summary page of the industrial production report. It
provides the latest monthly and annual changes in output. (The release
shows it was up 0.8% for the month of October and up 3.6% over the
year.) A black triangle near a number indicates a decline. Other pages
in the report (not included here) provide additional details on the
strength and weakness of individual sectors.

• Mining and Manufacturing: Shipments

\(2\) Industrial shipments represent actual sales and can be used to
determine demand. If shipments are increasing, this will likely lead to
further increases in production in the months ahead. Should shipments
begin to slacken, it will cause inventory levels to swell and discourage
future production. (In the table, shipments climbed 1.2% for the month
and 5.1% over the year.)

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei06.jpg)

</div>

• Mining and Manufacturing: Inventories and Inventory Ratios

\(3\) This section sheds light on the supply-and-demand pressures in the
industrial sector. A rise in the inventory index reflects the quantity
of goods produced that remains unsold. The inventory ratio index is
similar to the inventory-sales ratio in the U.S., except that it uses an
index rather than months of supply on hand. The ratio, which represents
inventories divided by shipments, can be a leading indicator of future
industrial output.

• Survey of Production Forecast

\(4\) Included in the industrial production release is a projection of
what output is expected to be the next two months. It’s a useful
addition because the numbers provide a sense of where the economy might
be heading. (The data in this table shows that production is predicted
to increase 3.1% in November but drop 0.9% in December.) This page also
breaks down the main components of production, enabling you to identify
which sectors will help raise output and which will drag it down. (For
example, General Machinery output is predicted to surge 18.7% in
November and fall 8.8% in December.) However, you should view this
forecast table with some skepticism. Projections historically tend to be
on the high side.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_376"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei08.jpg)

</div>

### <span id="ch04.html_page_377"></span><span id="ch04.html_page_378"></span>Japan’s Tankan Survey

**What Is It:** A widely anticipated report on business confidence in
Japan.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.boj.or.jp/en/statistics/tk/index.htm/](http://www.boj.or.jp/en/statistics/tk/index.htm/)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.boj.or.jp/en/](http://www.boj.or.jp/en/)*

**Release Time:** 8:50 a.m. (local time); results are published at the
start of April, July, and October, and in mid-December.

**Frequency:** Quarterly.

**Source:** Bank of Japan.

**Revisions:** Statistical corrections are rare. Revisions merely
reflect changes in confidence and plans from one quarter to the next.

Aside from the U.S., Japan has arguably the most extensive collection of
economic indicators in the world, much of it in English and freely
available on the Web. Perhaps that’s to be expected from the
third-largest economy (after the United States and China). Among the
reports Japan churns out is the Tankan survey, which has gained
worldwide recognition for its sweeping coverage, forward-looking
features, and quick release to the public. International investors and
managers of multinational companies look to the Tankan report for the
latest reading on the state of the Japanese economy and its forecasts of
business activity in the months ahead. What gives this survey extra
credibility is the agency behind it. The Tankan survey is produced by
the Bank of Japan, the country’s central bank, and its results can be
used to formulate future monetary policy. As a result, this closely
watched quarterly report has a history of moving stock prices and
currencies.

Often described as a business confidence survey, the Tankan survey is
really much more than that. Indeed, this report offers more insight into
what the business community is thinking than does any comparable U.S.
economic indicator. If you want to know about Japanese plans for future
capital investments, employment, or expectations of pricing power, and
predictions of where the yen will likely be valued in the future, this
release covers all this and a lot more.

The survey itself is conducted quarterly by the Research and Statistics
Department at the Bank of Japan. Questionnaires are sent out the last
month of every quarter—March, June, September, and December—to about
11,000 firms. These companies are differentiated by their size—large (on
average 22% of the sample), medium (27%), and small (51%)—and by
industry type, with more going to nonmanufacturers (60%) than to
manufacturing (40%). Amazingly, the response rate of these surveys tends
to be better than 98%!

<span id="ch04.html_page_379"></span>Respondents are asked to answer
eight broad questions:

**1.** Business conditions (favorable or unfavorable?)

**2.** Supply-and-demand conditions (excessive demand or excessive
supply?), inventories (excessive or insufficient?), and prices (rising
or falling?)

**3.** Sales and current profits (% change)

**4.** Fixed investment at non-financial institutions (% change)

**5.** Fixed investments at financial institutions (%)

**6.** Employment (excessive employment or insufficient?)

**7.** Corporate finance (easy or tight monetary conditions?)

**8.** Business conditions at financial institutions (favorable or
unfavorable?)

Of the eight topics, five seek qualitative assessments that require a
judgment call (topics 1, 2, 6, 7, and 8). After these responses are
collected, a diffusion index is computed by simply calculating the
percentage of businesses reporting a negative tone and subtracting it
from the percentage indicating a positive tone. The remaining three
questions (3, 4, and 5) ask for quantitative changes in percentage terms
regarding recent performance, as well as expectations about how this
will change in the future.

The following sections highlight a few of the most useful tables in the
Tankan survey.

• Business Conditions for Large Manufacturers

\(1\) Manufacturing is one of the main engines of growth in Japan
because it includes the country’s vital export industry. In this table,
we see confidence improved in December (actual result) to a net 11,
representing a 10-percentage-point gain in confidence from September’s
survey. However, these same manufacturers have predicted a slight
deterioration in conditions in the next few months, because the
diffusion index on the forecast dropped back to 8.

Aside from the summary number at the top of the table, confidence levels
are also broken down into broad industry categories such as motor
vehicles and industrial machinery.

• Business Conditions for Nonmanufacturers

\(2\) This section is a good measure of the strength of consumer demand
in Japan. Large nonmanufacturers conduct most of their business in the
country and do not benefit much from strong export growth. One can look
at the headline figure to get an idea of domestic demand, as well as how
specific sectors are doing. For example, retailers noted that conditions
barely improved over the past quarter, moving from –14 to –13. Note,
however, that more of them appeared optimistic about conditions in the
subsequent three months because the forecast index rose to –5.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_380"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei09.jpg)

</div>

<span id="ch04.html_page_381"></span>• Business Conditions at Small
Enterprises

\(3\) Are all businesses benefiting from economic growth, or just a few?
How widespread is the recovery in Japan? By comparing the sentiment
levels of large and small companies, one can tell whether businesses
across the board are seeing an improvement in sales and profits—or if
these gains are limited to mainly large enterprises.

• Average Exchange Rates Predicted by Large Manufacturers

\(4\) How the yen is valued in relation to other currencies can make all
the difference in how successful Japanese exporters are at selling
products in foreign markets. This table represents the best guess by
major Japanese manufacturers as to what value the yen will average in
the first and second halves of the year, as well as for the year as a
whole. Indeed, there is a correlation between how cheap the yen is
expected to be and the level of business confidence by large
manufacturers. The lower the yen’s value in foreign exchange markets,
the more upbeat manufacturers become because it effectively drops the
price of Japanese-made goods abroad.

• Prices by Large Enterprises

\(5\) Companies that can raise prices generally achieve higher earnings
and hire more workers. However, there are times when businesses find it
difficult to lift prices. Either competition prevents them from doing
so, or the economy is undergoing a deflationary spiral in which prices
are under continuous pressure to fall. The latter has been a serious
problem with Japan throughout the 1990s and beyond. This index
represents the percentage of companies saying their prices had risen
versus those that lowered prices. The numbers show that slightly more
firms in the latest survey have raised prices. The index for large
manufacturers inched up from –23 in September to –21 in the December
survey. But that might prove to be just a brief reprieve because the
expectations index fell back to –24.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei10.jpg)

</div>

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei11.jpg)

</div>

• Fixed Investment

\(6\) Capital spending is another major contributor to economic growth.
It serves as a marker of confidence that companies have about future
business activity. Here we see large manufacturers planning to boost
investment spending by 11.1% in Japan’s 2003 fiscal year, compared to
what was spent the previous year.

<span id="ch04.html_page_382"></span>• Production Capacity

\(7\) Lots of unused factory capacity poses problems for an economy. It
will depress business spending in the future and perhaps even lead to
plant closings and layoffs. In contrast, a reduction in excess plant
capacity suggests that customer
<span id="ch04.html_page_383"></span>orders are rising and more
factories are being utilized to satisfy this demand. The diffusion index
shows the net percentage of companies that claim to have too much excess
capacity. Figures here show that fewer companies are experiencing idle
assembly lines; the index for excessive capacity fell from 17 to 14. The
forecast is for even greater use of existing capacity, since the number
is expected to drop to 12.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei12.jpg)

</div>

As rich as the Tankan survey is with information on the private business
sector in Japan, there are two cautionary points to consider. First,
since the powerful Bank of Japan is behind this report, the firms
queried are aware that their responses might have a bearing on monetary
policy by the central bank. Therefore, respondents could be tempted to
shape their answers in a way that can result in a favorable
interest-rate policy. Second, a large part of the survey depends on
forecasts, which might turn out to be inaccurate. Aside from these
caveats, the Tankan survey is viewed by the international investment
community as a valuable and well-regarded economic report.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_384"></span>Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) by Country and Region

**What Is It:** A timely series of reports on manufacturing activity in
different countries and regions.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.markiteconomics.com/Survey/Page.mvc/PressReleases](http://www.markiteconomics.com/Survey/Page.mvc/PressReleases)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.ntc-research.com/](http://www.ntc-research.com/)*

**Release Time:** Varies with different countries. A schedule of
upcoming releases can be viewed here:
*[www.markiteconomics.com/Survey/Page.mvc/DiaryofReleaseDates](http://www.markiteconomics.com/Survey/Page.mvc/DiaryofReleaseDates)*

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Sources:** Markit Economics (formerly NTC Economics), J.P. Morgan,
HSBC Holdings plc, Institute for Supply Management (ISM), International
Federation of Purchasing and Supply Management (IFPSM).

**Revisions:** Markit Economics does not revise the monthly survey data
after the first publication. However, seasonal adjustment factors are
revised from time to time.

The popularity of the U.S. purchasing manager surveys has spawned a
bunch of similar measures in other countries. The U.S. Purchasing
Managers Index (PMI) for manufacturing, produced by the Institute for
Supply Management, is one of the hottest economic indicators out every
month. It has demonstrated a solid track record of anticipating turning
points in the business cycle and for being way ahead of the curve in
detecting a buildup of inflation pressures. Indeed, it is so highly
regarded by investors, economists, and policymakers that many other
nations have developed their own PMI series in recent years, all
basically modeled after the U.S. The purchasing managers survey was
launched in the U.K. in 1991, followed by Germany (1996), France (1998),
Japan (2002), and China (2005). All told, purchasing manager indexes are
available for more than two dozen countries and they can tell us quite a
lot about activity in these individual countries and, together, the
strength of the global economy.

Collecting all this data is a London-based firm called Markit Economics.
When it comes to global economic intelligence, few companies can match
the vast array of financial, business, and economic information it
provides. For the Purchasing Managers series, the firm gathers data from
more than 16,000 companies across more than 20 countries every month,
and seeks to track activity in manufacturing, services, retail, and
construction sectors. In addition to producing a PMI for the Eurozone,
Markit Economics teamed up with HSBC, another global financial services
company, to come up with a PMI series of China, and with J.P. Morgan for
a global PMI—and the results for all can be seen on Markit Economics’
Web site.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_385"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei13.jpg)

</div>

We’ll focus on three of the most eagerly awaited international PMI
manufacturing reports: one on the Eurozone, a Global index, and one on
China.

#### Eurozone Manufacturing PMI

Established in 1997, the Eurozone Manufacturing PMI is one of the first
composite indicators out every month on conditions in eight countries:
Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Ireland, Greece, Austria, and the
Netherlands. They represent 92% of all manufacturing activity in the
euro currency area. The report is based on responses from 3,000
purchasing executives. Markit Economics collects the data from the
individual national surveys as well and then recomputes a regional index
for each of the major questions asked. Finally, an overall headline
index is calculated to reflect total manufacturing activity in the
region.

At the heart of the surveys are questions to purchasing managers that
cover six key themes:

<span id="ch04.html_page_386"></span>**1.** Is the level of new orders
received by your company higher than, the same as, or lower than one
month ago?

This question addresses the issue of demand in the economy. If demand
for goods increases, it will drive up manufacturing output.

**2.** Is the level of output in your company higher than, the same as,
or lower than one month ago?

The focus here is on whether there’s been a shift in production to
higher levels because of new orders.

**3.** Is the stock of items purchased by your company higher than, the
same as, or lower than one month ago?

For manufacturers to keep their production lines running smoothly, they
need to have an ample supply of raw materials on hand. But as output
accelerates, supplies typically diminish and purchasing managers need to
reorder more stock. Thus, the purchase of new items is linked to the
pace of production.

**4.** Are supplier delivery times experienced by your company longer
than, the same as, or shorter than one month ago?

Just because a purchasing manager places an order to replenish its stock
of raw materials doesn’t necessarily mean it will arrive overnight.
Suppliers generally can ship raw materials to manufacturers faster in a
slow economy. In a booming economy, however, when lots of orders for raw
materials are coming in at the same time, suppliers can’t instantly
satisfy all the demand. Bottlenecks emerge, and even suppliers have
their own production constraints. As a result, shipments to
manufacturers slow and this leads to delays in deliveries. Thus, longer
lead times between orders and deliveries of raw materials are a sign of
faster economic growth, whereas rapid deliveries suggest slower business
activity.

**5.** Is the average input price experienced by your company higher
than, the same as, or lower than one month ago?

It should come as no surprise that when many manufacturers increase
orders simultaneously, demand for raw materials can outstrip supplies.
This places upward pressure on factory input prices.

**6.** Is the level of employment at your company higher than, the same
as, or lower than one month ago?

There is a link between employment in manufacturing and production.
Greater demand for new orders often leads to more employment. However,
over time, the relationship between jobs and output turns more tenuous.
Given the high cost of labor, manufacturers might try investing more in
improving productivity than in expanding their workforce to raise
output. Thus, production could increase at a faster pace than job growth
in the long run.

<span id="ch04.html_page_387"></span>The results are presented in the
form of a diffusion index. A reading of less than 50 indicates a
contraction of activity, above 50 points to an expansion, and an index
of exactly 50 says that no change has occurred.

In addition, an aggregate index is computed using a weighted average of
five (of the six) queries above. It is based on the following formula:
The new orders response is given a 30% weight, output 25%, employment
20%, supplier delivery times 15%, and stocks of items purchased 10%.
You’ll notice that the PMI index on prices is left out of the equation.
Though input prices are a very good leading indicator of producer price
inflation, changes in prices can occur for many reasons that have
nothing to do with the business cycle. Strikes, currency movements,
restrictions in supplies by foreign producers, and bizarre weather all
influence input prices of raw materials regardless of the pace of
economic activity. As a result, the change in price data is excluded
from the total survey index.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei14.jpg)

</div>

*Source:* Markit Economics, used with permission.

#### Global Manufacturing PMI

First released in October 2003, the Global PMI series wants to be
considered a gauge of world manufacturing trends. It functions the same
way as the Eurozone purchasing managers report, except that it includes
a larger sample. J.P. Morgan and Markit Economics have worked together
to collect responses from 9,000 purchasing managers in 30 countries that
collectively represent 86% of the world’s total manufacturing output.
Again, what makes this report so useful are the questions asked; they
inquire about real activity (specifically, output, new orders, input
prices, and employment) and do not solicit personal or subjective views.
A reading of 50 indicates no change from the preceding month. Below 50
is a sign of contraction, and above 50 points to an expansion.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei15.jpg)

</div>

*Source:* Markit Economics, JP Morgan Chase Bank, used with permission.

I should add that in addition to a manufacturing index, there are also
separate releases on activity in the service sector for the Eurozone and
Global PMIs. Services account for a predominant share of the GDP in most
modern industrial economies. Although that’s not the case with the large
emerging countries, even they have seen services grab an increasingly
larger share of their economies in recent years.

So which PMI series—manufacturing or services—can better foreshadow
economic turning points? For Europe the answer appears to be the
purchasing managers index for services since there is evidence that this
index has a better correlation with changes in GDP than the
manufacturing PMI. But if you are trying to anticipate shifts in
“global” economic activity, most investors still track the global
manufacturing PMI. The reason is that for the U.S. and in most
developing countries, the goods-producing sector tends to respond more
immediately to changes in demand than services. However, given the
dynamic growth in services worldwide, you can expect the Global PMI
Services Index to match the influence of its manufacturing cousin over
the next decade.

<span id="ch04.html_page_388"></span><span id="ch04.html_page_389"></span>Finally,
getting Eurozone and Global PMI data from the Internet is relatively
easy, though the amount of free information provided is limited. Details
on both series are available primarily to clients. Nevertheless, there
is some useful material on the Web that makes it worthwhile to check
out.

#### <span id="ch04.html_page_390"></span>China Manufacturing PMI

Thanks to the combined efforts of HSBC and Markit Economics, we are now
able to get more precise economic data on China, and it couldn’t come at
a more important time. For the past three decades, China has been the
fastest-growing economy on the planet. What’s truly mind-boggling is
that it took just five years for the country to cruise past the United
Kingdom, Germany, and Japan to become the second-largest economy in the
world. Some have argued that China is now within a generation of
exceeding even the U.S. If so, it wouldn’t be unprecedented. For much of
recorded history, China had the largest economy in the world, before it
flamed out in the 19<sup>th</sup> century and most of the
20<sup>th</sup> century as civil wars, conflicts with Japan, and the
reign of Mao Zedong damaged the country. Since 1978, however, it has
bounced back in spectacular fashion, and China is once again a palpable
force in the global economy.

Today, investors, economists, business leaders, and policymakers spend
as much time wondering about the economic outlook in China as they do
the U.S. and Europe. One important metric that helps analysts understand
the underlying momentum driving the Chinese economy is the HSBC/Markit
Economics monthly report on China’s Purchasing Manager’s Manufacturing
Activity Index. This survey is based on replies from purchasing managers
representing more than 400 small, medium, and large manufacturers in
China, including both private and state-owned enterprises. HSBC then
releases two PMI reports on China each month. The first is the “Flash”
report, based on 85% to 90% of the survey responses. That is followed a
week later with a “Final” PMI. Both publish diffusion indexes on
manufacturing output, new orders, new export orders, employment,
backlogs of work, prices, inventory of finished goods, quantity of
purchases, and delivery times.

(The HSBC/Markit Economics PMI report on China should not be confused
with China’s own purchasing managers series, which often comes out on
the same day. The country’s own National Bureau of Statistics and the
China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing use a larger sample and a
different methodology than HSBC to come up with its own purchasing
managers index. What happens when the two purchasing managers reports on
manufacturing head in different directions? In such circumstances, we
have to put greater weight on HSBC/Markit Economics series because their
methodology is more transparent than the government’s. In fact, no one
quite knows what goes into the government survey and that opaqueness
raises some skepticism about its validity.)

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei16.jpg)

</div>

*Source:* Markit Economics, used with permission.

The surprisingly quick acceptance by the public of purchasing manager
surveys as a whole comes at a time when there is much frustration with
the slow release of official economic statistics by governments. Some,
like the GDP, are published 60 to 70 days after the quarter ends.
Another complaint about official data is that countries use different
methods to come up with the same indicators. This complicates efforts to
make comparisons between economies. Finally, figures can be of such poor
quality that they are frequently followed by substantial revisions.

<span id="ch04.html_page_391"></span><span id="ch04.html_page_392"></span>In
contrast, the Eurozone, Global, and Chinese PMI series overseen by
Markit Economics employ the same basic methodology with all the
countries, so comparisons are much easier to make. What’s more,
revisions to the data are extremely rare. This is not to say that these
international surveys are without shortcomings. One problem is that they
make no effort to quantify the degree of change. For instance, if a
large number of purchasing managers say they witnessed just a modest
improvement in activity in the latest month, that alone is enough to
propel the index sharply higher. Nevertheless, the purchasing manager
series has gained a large following with investors and has on numerous
occasions moved markets with the release of its data.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_393"></span>OECD Composite Leading Indicators (CLI)

**What Is It:** A statistical guide to forecast business activity in the
world’s largest economies.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.oecd.org/std/cli](http://www.oecd.org/std/cli)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.oecd.org](http://www.oecd.org)*

**Release Time:** Noon (Continental time); data is released in the
second week of the month and refers to activity two months earlier. (For
example, January’s release reports leading indicators for November.)

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development
(OECD).

**Revisions:** The previous month’s data is frequently revised with each
new release.

Investors and policymakers love to follow leading economic indicators
because of their look-ahead qualities. They are supposed to predict
short-term movements in an economy by using measures that are highly
sensitive to upcoming changes in business conditions. The U.S. has its
own set of domestic leading economic indicators from the Conference
Board, a business research group in New York (see the section “[Index of
Leading Economic Indicators \[LEI\]](#ch03c.html_ch03clev1sec4)” in
[Chapter 3](#ch03a.html_ch03a), “[The Most Influential U.S. Economic
Indicators](#ch03a.html_ch03a)”). On a global scale, however, the
best-known and most closely studied equivalent is the OECD’s own
Composite Leading Indicators (CLI). This Paris-based international
organization computes a leading economic indicator index for 29 member
countries and 6 major nonmember nations. The regional zones covered are
the Total OECD area, the Eurozone currency area, the G7 countries, and
the Big Five Asian economies (see [Table 4.2](#ch04.html_ch04tab02)).
Although some countries produce their own in-house leading indicators,
it’s the OECD’s own indexes that make the big headlines and draw the
greatest interest among money managers and policymakers.

<span id="ch04.html_ch04tab02"></span>Table 4.2. OECD Groupings and
Other Regions in the Composite Leading Indicators

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04tab02.jpg)

</div>

Using economic data from its member countries, the OECD calculates CLI
indexes designed to forecast what’s ahead for industrial production in
the OECD nations and regions. Why industrial production and not the more
broad-based GDP? First, industrial output is seen as an effective proxy
for GDP because, historically, turning points in industrial production
have coincided with the overall economy. Second, using industrial
production as a reference point is more practical because that data
comes out every month, whereas the GDP is available only quarterly.

<span id="ch04.html_page_394"></span>Now for the obvious question: Does
the OECD’s CLI really work? Is it reliable in picking up signals of a
pending slowdown or rebound in economic growth? Here we get one of those
“Yes, but...” answers. To begin with, anticipating turning points is not
easy. Signs are often elusive or ambiguous. Second, much depends on the
quality of the underlying data from national governments, not to mention
the judgment calls involved in setting up the leading indicator models
and the assumptions behind them. By and large, the OECD’s leading
indicator series gets a thumbs-up from economists and large investors.
Even central bankers review the CLI data when setting interest-rate
policy for the euro currency zone. Over the years, the CLI has proven to
be an effective early-warning system, able to identify peaks and troughs
in economic activity some nine months in advance.

The OECD has been publishing the CLI since 1981, and the methodology is
fairly straightforward. Financial indicators with a reputation for being
ahead of the economic curve are chosen as components of this indicator.
Among the most common national components used by the OECD to calculate
the CLI are stock prices, building permits, monetary data, and
production orders. Indeed, more than 100 components are employed to come
up with a monthly ([Table 1](#ch04.html_tab01)) “Composite Leading
Indicators.”

\(1\) If there are three consecutive months of year-over-year negative
or positive changes, chances are the economy or a region is within 6 to
12 months of reaching a high or low point in economic activity.

\(2\) The OECD also provides a brief assessment on whether recent trends
in the Composite Leading Indicators signal an upcoming turning point in
the business cycle.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_395"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei17.jpg)

</div>

Easily the most eye-opening set of statistics the OECD makes available
are the macroeconomic indicators for most of the world’s major
economies. Besides the Composite Leading Indicators, you will also find
information on GDP, consumer prices, employment, and much more. It’s an
extraordinary Internet site by the OECD with a multitude of uses for
investors, business managers, and economists—and it is freely available!
That comprehensive database can be found at
*<http://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DatasetCode=MEI_CLI>*.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_396"></span>China Industrial Production
