**What Is It:** Measures the monthly change in China’s industrial
output.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*[www.stats.gov.cn/english/statisticaldata/monthlydata](http://www.stats.gov.cn/english/statisticaldata/monthlydata)*

**Home Web Address:**
*[www.stats.gov.cn/english](http://www.stats.gov.cn/english)*

**Release Time:** Between 10:00 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. (local time); the
report is first released in Chinese two weeks after the month ends.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS).

**Revisions:** Corrections to data may occur more frequently in the
future as China endeavors to improve the accuracy of its statistics.

Let’s begin with stating the obvious. China’s blazing economic progress
the past three decades has been unmatched by any country in modern
history. From the catastrophic social and economic failures of the
Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), China has managed to bounce back with
such ferocity that it seems the planet’s center of economic gravity has
shifted to the Far East. After all, no country produces more steel,
cement, mobile phones, color TVs, and cars. Indeed, one can argue that
given China’s manufacturing capabilities and its massive financial
resources, it is difficult to justify calling China an “emerging
economy.” The country has assembled several world-class industries,
including aviation, autos, and computers. Its technological prowess is
already a cut above that of most industrial countries. China owns the
second-fastest supercomputer, built the fastest passenger train in the
world, and has launched an astronaut into space, only the third country
to do so. All of this has helped catapult the People’s Republic of China
to become the world’s second-largest economy. These are hardly the
attributes of a struggling emerging country. China, of course, argues
that it has still not “emerged” enough to be classified an industrial
economy because its per capita GDP (the size of its economy divided by
population) remains among the lowest in the world, which is true. But
one fact is beyond dispute: China looms large as a genuine economic
superpower.

Certainly as a consumer market, China offers opportunities limited only
by imagination. Here is a nation of 1.3 billion people and growing,
including a labor force of more than 800 million, all eager to work and
spend money. Consumer demand has been climbing steadily the past two
decades as households have been driven to improve their standard of
living. That can be seen not only by their larger and better-furnished
residences, but also in the use of high-tech consumer products. Despite
government controls, China’s Internet population is now the largest in
the world, with more than 500 million citizens surfing the Web (as of
2012), an exponential jump from just 620,000 users 15 years earlier.

<span id="ch04.html_page_397"></span>The broader question is, what
intentions do China’s top political leaders have for the country?
Government officials talk about fortifying their “socialist market
economy,” a strange brew in which socialist ideals can be met in
conjunction with a more liberal, open, and capitalistic economy. What is
so interesting is that this bizarre mix has so far worked quite well for
China. Its economy has grown nearly 10% a year the past two decades.
Moreover, Chinese policymakers have successfully steered the country
away from several global economic storms, including the Asian financial
crisis and the Russian debt default in the late 1990s, the collapse of
the dot.com bubble (2000–01), and the 2008–09 global economic downturn.
They avoided these pitfalls largely because the government quickly
ordered policies that were designed to protect their economy from
outside shocks. Case in point: While other major economies were in
free-fall during the 2008–09 recession, the Chinese government quickly
implemented a nearly \$600 billion stimulus program. The result? At a
time when most other economies were shrinking, China’s GDP grew an
annual average of more than 7% from 2008 to 2010.

Impressive? Yes. But the absence of any parliamentary debate on economic
policy is not a practice to emulate. For there are also signs that
Communist China is starting to bump up against the limits of Capitalist
China. For instance, even though the country has grown much wealthier in
recent years, the inequality in income among its population is getting
wider and may incite more social unrest. All that spectacular growth has
simply not translated into greater prosperity for the vast majority of
its people. Indeed, inequality in China is growing at a faster rate than
in Brazil or India, according to the World Bank.

To reduce the income gap and address other economic problems, there is
evidence that China is creeping toward a more market-oriented economy.
More than half of the business sector is now in private hands. Concrete
steps are being taken to shift economic decision making away from a
centralized, command-style system. What’s more, China’s ascension to the
World Trade Organization in 2003 is supposed to bring its economic and
currency policies more in line with world standards, but that process
has been agonizingly slow so far. In the meantime, China’s rapid
expansion and massive consumer market continue to attract international
investors and multinational business leaders. Large foreign investment
bankers see in China a rich source of new clients as an increasing
number of companies there are being permitted to access global capital
markets to raise funds. Credit ratings firms, such as Standard & Poor’s,
Fitch, and Moody’s, are also charging into China to assess the
creditworthiness of its companies and government agencies. China itself
has become a major player in the international community. With a war
chest of more than \$3 trillion in foreign exchange reserves, by far the
largest in the world thanks to its cumulative trade surpluses, China is
in a position to buy huge chunks of foreign government bonds, stocks,
real estate, and other types of assets.

And yet, even with all the attributes that make it an economic
superpower, the country has at least one noticeable problem: Many
foreigners suspect that China puts out dubious statistics about its
economy. This poses a genuine problem for foreign firms and investors
who need to appraise the country’s current and future well-being.
Longtime <span id="ch04.html_page_398"></span>observers have complained
that China’s economic numbers are less accurate than those of other
industrialized countries, even going so far as to say that key officials
“cook the books” to impress foreign investors and lenders. In recent
years analysts have charged that China was overestimating its GDP growth
to lure foreign capital. At other times, there were accusations that
Chinese statisticians were intentionally underestimating growth to
create the impression that the economy was not overheating.

Behind these statistical problems lies an antiquated data collection
system, one that can be traced back to the old command economy days.
During the 1950s and 1960s, Communist party headquarters relied
extensively on production reports from local managers, who would often
lie about output figures to curry favor with party leaders. Small-town
Communist officials were often promoted based on the economic
performance in their region, so it was in their best interest to
embellish the figures. Thus, to some extent, the problem was not so much
at the headquarters level in Beijing, but with the field reports from
local and municipal managers. Today, China’s National Bureau of
Statistics (NBS) still gathers output figures much the same way as
before, though the fabrication is believed to be less widespread.
Nevertheless, China still has no independent method in place to check
the veracity of local production reports.

This doesn’t mean Beijing officials are sitting idle. They are well
aware that without a trustworthy source of economic information, it will
be hard for foreigners to make investment decisions or for Chinese
leaders to carry out the right fiscal and monetary policies. The NBS has
been working in earnest to upgrade the quality of its economic reports.
Among the modifications introduced recently was a change in the manner
in which statistics are collected. For example, Chinese officials
decided in March 2005 that data collectors should be placed under the
authority of the NBS. This can help redress many of the statistical
inaccuracies that originate from local municipalities. Second, the
government revamped how GDP is computed. This redesign was critical. The
traditional statistical reporting method failed to capture the growth
under way in the expanding service industries, such as real estate
agents, business consultants, and companies offering communication
services. To correct this shortcoming, the government conducted its
first-ever nationwide economic census in 2004, and the results were
startling. At the end of 2005, China announced that its economy was
actually much larger than previously thought. Virtually all of the
upward revision came from services, which turned out to represent more
than 40% of all economic activity, nearly 10 percentage points higher
than its prerevision share. It was fresh evidence that China’s economy
is becoming more diversified than first believed.

In 2011, the NBS took another important step to bring its economic
statistics more in line with Western standards. The agency began to
publish GDP growth rates on a quarterly basis, rather than just note how
output has changed from the same quarter a year ago. China has also
gotten much tougher with government employees who abuse the economic
data. When two officials sought to enrich themselves by leaking the
numbers on GDP, retail sales, and consumer price inflation before their
scheduled release, prosecutors cracked down hard by giving them stiff
prison sentences.

<div class="image">

<span id="ch04.html_page_399"></span>![Image](graphics/04sei18.jpg)

</div>

Another way that China has moved to bring its economic reports up to
global standards was to make the data more accessible to everyone in the
world. Here we see an earnest attempt by China’s NBS to construct a
user-friendly Web site with detailed information on economic output,
inflation, and other measures of performance, and much of it in English.
By going to the home page of the National Bureau of Statistics
([www.stats.gov.cn/english](http://www.stats.gov.cn/english)), one can
begin to stay on top of the country’s key economic data.

\(1\) Release Calendar: The NBS makes available an economic calendar for
key economic statistics.

\(2\) Statistical Data: High-frequency economic indicators—such as
retail sales, industrial production, consumer prices, and GDP—can be
found based on their schedule of releases.

<span id="ch04.html_page_400"></span>(3) Press Releases: A very good
start to get the latest economic data can be found here. View a sample
of a press release on industrial production below.

\(4\) NBS’s Press Release on Industrial production: Topping the list of
perhaps the best and most timely measures of economic performance in
China is its industrial production series. It measures changes in output
for the industrial sector of the economy, which includes manufacturing,
mining, and utilities. Industrial Production is a key metric for
economic forecasting and can anticipate changes in inflation. For
example, high levels of industrial production can heat up pricing
pressures and ultimately force the government to clamp down on output by
raising interest rates or curbing bank loan growth, or both. Every
month, the NBS issues a seven-page report on industrial output that
contains the latest official analysis, a detailed table of how key
sectors have performed, and graphics that illustrate how production and
its components performed over the past 12 months.

Anyone who wants to monitor the latest trends in China’s economy should
familiarize themselves with China’s NBS online Web site. Having said
that, we have to return to one big underlying concern. China does not do
itself any favors by keeping secret the methodology of how it computes
many of these economic indicators. To bolster public confidence in its
economic data, the government needs to be much more transparent on how
the data is gathered, what weights are being given to different sectoral
groups, and what calculations are used to compute these statistics.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_403"></span>India: Industrial Production and Inflation

**What Is It:** The two main indicators are among the most relevant in
monitoring India’s economy.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**
*<http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/site/inner.aspx?status=3&menu_id=84>*

**Home Web Address:** *<http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/site/Home.aspx>*

**Release Date:**

Industrial Production: Second week of the month.

The “New” Consumer Price Index: Third week of the month.

Wholesale Price Index: Second week of the month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Source:** Central Statistical Organization, Ministry of Statistics &
Programme Implementation.

India’s emergence as an economic power often gets overshadowed by its
giant neighbor to the east. That’s unfortunate. Not only is India coming
into its own, but many believe that the country will eventually surpass
China in both population and total output by 2050. What’s so compelling
about India is that its stunning growth since the early 1990s can be
traced to a strategy that sets it apart from other developing countries
in the region. From the beginning, India cleverly positioned itself so
that it did not have to compete head-to-head with China and the other
Asian countries. Indeed, what India did was defy the textbook path
toward economic development. Virtually all emerging countries in the
20<sup>th</sup> century used their cheap labor and whatever capital they
could scrape together to build up their manufacturing or agricultural
capabilities. Exports and construction became the key drivers of
economic growth for these countries.

However, India followed a strikingly different road by capitalizing on
its own unique comparative advantage. India, like China, enjoys a large
population (1.2 billion versus 1.3 billion for China), but the
characteristics of these two groups differ in important respects.
India’s labor force is younger, is more traveled, and speaks English.
Given these attributes, business leaders concluded that economic success
would more likely come from services, and less from manufacturing. As a
result, the country now offers a panoply of important services to the
world, including banking, insurance, engineering, media, software,
business outsourcing, medical diagnostics, telecommunications, and film
entertainment. (India’s film industry, for example, is the biggest in
the world, in both the number of movies produced and the number of
tickets sold.)

India has thus bucked the trend by choosing to rely more on services
than manufacturing or natural resources as a means to achieve healthy
economic growth. This decision has propelled its \$1.7 trillion economy
to be the third largest in Asia and eleventh largest in the world.
Moreover, India’s blistering growth rate has led to an escalation in
wages <span id="ch04.html_page_404"></span>among service-sector
employees, and especially for skilled workers. This has enhanced family
income and stimulated domestic demand. To give you a sense of how
rapidly the country is changing, back in 1991, India had a total of five
million telephone lines in the country. Now it is adding five million
new phone connections each month!

One of the burning questions investors ask is whether India’s economy
can continue to race ahead as it has. Can it conceivably even overtake
China in total output? The answer to both questions is yes, though the
latter is probably a few decades away. India’s prospects look bright for
several reasons. First, the country has undertaken substantial political
and economic reforms the past two decades. It has rejected socialism,
opened its economy to more imports, deregulated industries, allowed the
rupee to float more freely, and reduced barriers to trade.

Second, India’s leaders also realized that the country cannot depend on
services forever to keep its economy robust. And they certainly do not
want the country to be viewed as simply a back-office operation for
American companies that consists mainly of call centers, customer help
lines, and computer programmers. So fresh domestic and foreign capital
has also been directed to establish a sophisticated manufacturing
industry, one that utilizes state-of-the-art technology and embraces the
latest techniques of just-in-time inventory. The results have so far
been impressive. India’s annual growth in manufacturing is now
accelerating at about the same pace as services. All told, India’s
service industry accounts for 63% of the GDP; the industrial sector
contributes 20%; and agriculture, which was the backbone of its economy
shortly after the country gained independence, has now taken a back seat
in the 21<sup>st</sup> century and contributes only 17% to the GDP.

Given the country’s extraordinary economic accomplishments,
international investors are making the inevitable comparisons with
China. Though China’s economy is four times the size of India’s, the
question often asked is, who really will have the edge in the years
ahead?

Certainly both countries have enormous potential to grow and prosper.
But there are some important differences between them that might shape
their economic destiny:

• Cultural purists may yell and scream about it, but the fact remains
that English is the language of international business. In this respect,
India has a big advantage over China. The medium of communication in
India’s colleges and universities is English. Indeed, India is the
world’s largest English-speaking country. The ability of workers and
management to effectively communicate with customers and investors
around the world is critically important to attract foreign capital and
to find new markets for Indian-made products.

• India has a long tradition of democracy and known for having a
transparent legal system. In contrast, China, while it has made some
strides to decentralize its economy and allow more local autonomy, is
still run by an autocratic Communist leadership. Its legal system is far
from a model of transparency, and its courts are subject to political
pressure. What’s more, social unrest has increased in China,
<span id="ch04.html_page_405"></span>especially in rural farm areas.
Such strife is symptomatic of a country that is struggling to pursue two
inherently conflicting goals: allowing more market capitalism in the
economy, and preserving its Communist political heritage and the
ideologies that stem from it. The social tension that comes from
pursuing two incongruous objectives is not expected to subside anytime
soon. With so much uncertainty about China’s long-term stability,
investors may place greater faith in the future of a more open India.

• No economy can prosper unless it has a healthy banking system that can
finance consumer and business activity. India’s banking system, though
much smaller than China’s in terms of assets, is far healthier and
better capitalized. India’s loans, for example, are priced according to
risk, so interest rates tend to be higher than those in China. China has
historically chosen to keep rates artificially low, in part because
policymakers want to keep its currency (the yuan) undervalued. However,
that has also allowed Chinese banks to issue such artificially
low-interest-rate loans to domestic borrowers, including failing
state-owned enterprises, and that raises questions about the future
viability of such loans. Keep in mind that China has had to bail out its
banks more than once in the past decade. Meanwhile, India’s regulators
appear determined to keep its banks financially sound from the outset.
They demand high capital requirements for lenders and make sure that
these institutions have sufficient provisions set aside against bad
loans.

• Unlike India, China faces a serious demographic squeeze in coming
years. The Communist country has implemented a “one family, one child”
policy, and Chinese households have mostly adhered to it. As a result,
birthrates and family sizes have been shrinking since 1980. No such
policy exists in India; consequently, its population is much younger on
average and more dynamic. Experts predict that India will end up with a
larger population than China in the next five years or so. If that trend
materializes, it will have profound implications for both countries. As
China struggles to service an aging workforce that draws down national
savings, India will enjoy a more youthful, active, and prosperous labor
force. This can help catapult India’s economy past China by midcentury.

But it’s not all smooth sailing for India. If the economy is ever to
meet its full potential, India will first have to address some serious
internal shortcomings. One is the critical need to upgrade its creaking
infrastructure. India’s road transportation system is in dismal shape.
Highways make up less than 5% of its road network, and this makes it
tough to transport goods around the country. In addition, there is a
critical shortage of lodging facilities, and this has hurt both tourism
and foreign business travel in the country. There were only 140,000
hotel rooms in all of India in 2011, whereas China had more than ten
times as many. Also in dire need of expansion are India’s ports. There
are not enough of them to handle all the merchant ships that arrive and
leave with goods, and this has hampered the flow of both imports and
exports. Government officials also have to beef up the
<span id="ch04.html_page_406"></span>nation’s power-generating system.
Right now India does not have enough plants to satisfy the electrical
demands of a fast-growing economy. Blackouts are not uncommon, even in
Bangalore, where the country’s high-tech computer and software industry
is situated.

Aside from having a lagging infrastructure, India continues to be
stigmatized by its stifling bureaucracy, red tape, corruption, and set
of rigid labor rules that makes it quite difficult for companies to lay
off employees. Unless these deficiencies and administrative problems are
corrected, India will have great difficulty achieving world-class
economic status.

If the government fails to follow up with the needed public investments,
it will stunt the economy’s growth for years and probably bring higher
rates of inflation. On the other hand, if officials allocate enough
resources to improve roads, ports, electrical generation, and airports,
as well as reduce bureaucratic delays, the benefits will be lasting and
significant. Whichever course the country takes, the results will show
up in the macroeconomic data, particularly with industrial production
and inflation. To monitor these and other key economic indicators of
India, one can go online to the Ministry of Statistics—specifically, the
Central Statistical Organization (CSO).

The latest data on the major macroeconomic indicators has been assembled
on one page, found at
<http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/site/inner.aspx?status=3&menu_id=84>.

The Web page breaks down as follows:

**1.** *GDP at current prices.*

**2.** *GDP at constant prices.* (To view the entire press release of
the latest quarterly GDP report, go to
<http://mospi.nic.in/Mospi_New/upload/mospi_press_releases.htm?status=1&menu_id=120>.)

**3.** *The key components of GDP.*

**4.** *Industrial production:* Total and broken down by its three major
segments: mining, manufacturing, and electricity. But more revealing are
the three main categories of product: capital goods, intermediate goods,
and consumer goods.

**5.** *Inflation:* The CSO publishes a dizzying array of inflation
measures, seven to be exact. They are the GDP implicit price index, no
fewer than five variants of consumer price inflation, and the wholesale
price index (WPI).

The implicit price index is a quarterly measure and thus is not
especially timely. Of the five CPI measures, the three most useful are
the recently introduced groupings of CPI Urban (which is based on
surveys taken from 310 towns), CPI rural (based on 1,181 villages across
India), and the combined CPI (a series that began in 2012 and serves as
the headline retail price inflation in the country). The newly
constructed national CPI will likely replace the wholesale price index
as the main benchmark for monetary policy action by India’s central
bank. For years, the Reserve Bank of India had relied on the wholesale
price index as a barometer of price pressures in the country. But
critics complained that the WPI often understated inflation because it
looked only at product <span id="ch04.html_page_407"></span>prices at
the wholesale level and largely ignored the cost of services, a sector
that plays an increasingly important role in the economy. Economists in
India took note of how the rest of the world focused on the CPI because
it ultimately reflected prices to the end user, namely consumers. As a
result, we believe that the three CPI measures will in time overshadow
the WPI as the best leading indicator of monetary policy.

**6.** *Wholesale Price Index (WPI):* India’s WPI is similar to the
Producer Price Index in other countries. It is sensitive to price
changes in commodities and industrial goods but, as stated previously,
has little representation in services.

### <span id="ch04.html_page_410"></span>Brazil’s Industrial Production and the IBC-BR Economic Activity Index

**What Is It:** Two important economic statistics on Brazil. The first
reflects industrial output, and the second is considered a leading
indicator of the country’s GDP.

**News Release on the Internet:**

Industrial Production:
*[www.ibge.gov.br/english/presidencia/default_ant.php](http://www.ibge.gov.br/english/presidencia/default_ant.php)*
and *[www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS](http://www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS)*

IBC-Br Economic Activity Index:
*[www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS](http://www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS)*

**Release Time:**

Industrial Production: 9:30 a.m.(local time); the report is released
about 40 days after the survey month ends. (Thus, January’s release
refers to industrial performance in November.)

IBC-Br Economic Activity Index: 10:20 a.m. (local time); published about
45 days after the reference month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Sources:** Brazilian National Statistics Institute, Brazilian
Institute for Geography and Statistics (IBGE), and the Central Bank of
Brazil.

**Revisions:** Both reports are subject to revisions.

There is no country on the planet—not a single developing or industrial
nation—that possesses the near-perfect set of attributes Brazil has. And
if you suspect I’m guilty of hyperbole here, think again. Brazil may be
classified as an emerging economy, but it also has as a well-diversified
industrial sector—including one of the largest aerospace industries in
the world, a major auto producer, a global-size energy company—and has
the engineering know-how and resources to even build a nuclear
submarine. But let’s not stop there. Brazil is endowed with a
mind-boggling array of physical and natural resources, thanks to the
Amazon basin. It is energy self-sufficient (a fact that bears repeating
for emphasis), has ample arable land, possesses massive offshore oil
fields, enjoys a benign climate, is gifted with thousands of miles of
magnificent beaches, and is surrounded by other democratically elected
developing nations. To many foreign investors, Brazil just about defines
what the “promised land” should look like.

The country thus has all the prerequisites to become a prosperous leader
in the global economy, and that has not escaped the attention of foreign
investors. Indeed, many look upon Brazil as having even greater economic
potential than the two Asian giants. China might have matchless human
assets with 1.3 billion people (versus Brazil’s more modest 200 million
citizens), but it also is rapidly running out of critical natural
resources. India has a large population and a fast-growing economy, but
it too is highly dependent on imports of oil and other vital
commodities. Looked at in terms of per capita GDP (a way of measuring a
country’s <span id="ch04.html_page_411"></span>standard of living),
Brazil recorded a per capita GDP of \$11,769 in 2011, far higher than
that of China (\$8,382) and three times that of India (\$3,694),
according to the IMF.

In many respects, Brazil is already a star player in the global arena.
It has just surpassed Britain to become the world’s sixth-largest
economy. Closer to home, Brazil easily outweighs its neighbors in
economic size, accounting for more than 40% of Latin America’s total
GDP.

Facilitating all this progress have been the political and economic
reforms the country has undertaken the past three decades. After more
than half a century of strong military influence in the government, the
country made a fateful transition to mass electoral democracy in the
mid-1980s. This shift was all the more remarkable because it occurred
smack in the middle of the Latin American debt crisis. In addition to
establishing a vigorous democracy with a multiparty system, Brazil’s
leaders have liberalized the domestic capital markets. They allowed
their currency to float in foreign exchange markets, crafted a new
fiscal spending plan, opened the economy to more competition, embarked
on a privatization program, and passed legislation to further deregulate
the economy. Moreover, in a bold forward-looking move, policymakers
successfully placed the country on a path toward energy independence.
Brazil’s ethanol program, along with newfound oil, transformed the
country from being a net importer of oil in the 1980s to one that is
energy self-sufficient in 2006, and now destined to be a major oil
exporter.

The results for Brazil’s economy have been palpable. The country has
weathered global economic downturns better than its neighbors. While the
U.S. and Europe struggled with recession after the tech-bubble burst of
2000 and 2001, economic activity in Brazil continued to expand without
interruption. It even weathered the global financial downturn of 2008–09
with relatively minor damage. The country was one of the last to fall
into recession in 2008 but among the first to resume growth in 2009. In
fact, Brazil’s GDP bounced back with a robust 7.5% growth rate in 2010
and a respectable 2.7% in 2011 (beating out the performance of the U.S.
and Europe).

Still, Brazil needs to do more. Its central bank, which carries out
monetary policy, does not yet have full independence and thus can be
subject to political influence. The country continues to have severe
social problems due to sharp inequalities in its income distribution. It
also has a creaky infrastructure that requires attention, and it needs
to further reform its judicial system.

But make no mistake: Brazil’s economy is on the move and international
investors have eagerly returned to help expand the country’s industrial
and service sectors. Anyone monitoring economic activity in Brazil has
to focus on at least two key indicators: industrial production and the
IBC-Br Economic Activity Index.

#### Industrial Production

The first important indicator is industrial production, which represents
27% of the country’s GDP (with services contributing 67% and agriculture
6%). To measure industrial <span id="ch04.html_page_412"></span>output,
the government surveys 8,500 establishments on the output of 900
different products. Brazil’s Institute for Geography and Statistics
(IBGE) compiles the data, announces the news, and publishes an online
press release in English. There are two excellent online sources to view
the latest data on Brazil’s industrial production.

One source is IBGE’s Web site
(*[www.ibge.gov.br/english/presidencia/default_ant.php](http://www.ibge.gov.br/english/presidencia/default_ant.php)*),
shown here.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei23a.jpg)

</div>

Another government agency, the Central Bank of Brazil
(*[www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS](http://www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS)*),
does a slightly better job of presenting the industrial production
tables along with other important economic indicators—though without any
accompanying commentary. What’s more, the information has to be
downloaded onto a spreadsheet, but it’s a step well worth the effort.

<span id="ch04.html_page_413"></span>After the data is downloaded from
Brazil’s central bank, the top part of the page notes the monthly
value-added index of industrial production, and the bottom has all the
percentage changes with the following time frames:

• The latest monthly change (using seasonally adjusted figures).

• Change over the past 12 months (using the observed data, not
seasonally adjusted).

• Change in the year so far versus the same period the previous year
(using observed data).

• Change in the past 12 months from the prior 12 months (using observed
data).

The page also breaks down industrial production as follows:

• General industrial production index: An overall snapshot of industrial
output.

• Capital goods: An indicator that tells whether companies are
investing.

• Intermediate goods: A helpful leading sign of future production.

• Consumer durable goods: A category that consists of household
appliances and home electronics.

• Consumer nondurable goods: Here we refer mainly to food and clothing.
Both consumer durable and nondurable goods output are linked to the
growth in wages and personal income.

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei24.jpg)

</div>

#### The IBC-Br Economic Activity Index

The second key indicator on Brazil is the IBC-Br Economic Activity Index
(*[www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS](http://www.bcb.gov.br/?INDICATORS)*).
It’s published monthly by Brazil’s central bank and is closely watched
by analysts who consider it a reliable leading indicator of the
country’s quarterly GDP performance. The Economic Activity Index was
originally released as a regional statistic, but the central bank
expanded its coverage to the national economy in 2010. The index now
incorporates estimates for the monthly output of Brazil’s three
sectors—industrial, services, and agriculture—and computes an index
using a methodology similar to calculating the GDP. By tracking both
industrial production and the Economic Activity Index, investors can get
an excellent overview on the health of the Brazilian economy and its
likely direction.

<div class="image">

### <span id="ch04.html_page_415"></span><span id="ch04.html_page_416"></span>Canada: International Merchandise Trade Composite Leading Indicators Ivey Purchasing Managers Index

**What Is It:** Three economic measures on Canada that move markets.

**Home Web Address for Statistics Canada:**
*[www.statcan.gc.ca/start-debut-eng.html](http://www.statcan.gc.ca/start-debut-eng.html)*

**Home Web Address for Ivey Purchasing Managers Index:**
*<http://iveypmi.uwo.ca/english/index.htm>*

**Release Time:**

International Merchandise Trade: 8:30 a.m. (ET); released the second
week of each month.

Composite Leading Indicators: 8:30 a.m. (ET); released the third week of
each month.

Ivey Purchasing Managers Index: 10:00 a.m. (ET); released the fourth
working day of the following month.

**Frequency:** Monthly.

**Sources:** Statistics Canada; Richard Ivey School of Business, Western
University, Canada.

We have all heard of the “stress tests” that regulators imposed on U.S.
banks recently to determine whether they can survive future economic
shocks. The tests involve putting banks through a series of
near-cataclysmic scenarios to see how financially sturdy they are. It’s
an imperative exercise to prevent future bailouts by taxpayers. But
here’s a question: Why waste a perfectly horrendous financial crisis?
Let’s look back and see which major industrial economies and banks came
out of the 2008–09 global catastrophe relatively unscathed. After all,
*that* event was the ultimate stress test, so wouldn’t it be interesting
to see who passed through this devastating experience with minimal
damage?

It turns out only two advanced countries came through in good form,
Canada and Australia. We’ll begin with Canada and discuss Australia in
the next section.

What is so appealing about Canada is its enormous economic diversity and
overall financial soundness—a combination all too rare these days. By
economic diversity, I mean to highlight both the wealth of its natural
resources *and* the country’s highly skilled workforce in manufacturing
and services. When it comes to financial soundness, we look to the
integrity of the banking industry, because no economy can function well
without a vibrant group of banks to help finance economic activity.
Let’s view each separately.

Canada’s economy can be divided into three distinct sectors: resources,
manufacturing, and services.

#### <span id="ch04.html_page_417"></span>Resources

That it has such a vast assortment of natural resources should not come
as a complete surprise since the country has the second-largest landmass
in the world (exceeded only by Russia). Central and western Canada in
particular have seen rapid growth in the production of oil, lumber,
diamonds, gold, nickel and uranium—to make the short list. Yet even
parts of eastern Canada, like Newfoundland and Labrador, areas that long
relied on the fishing industry for income, are now leading the way with
new oil and gas exploration. And it is all paying off. Canada has the
third-largest proven oil reserves in the world (more than Kuwait and
Russia *combined*). It is also the eighth-largest oil exporter, shipping
more crude than half the OPEC countries.

#### Manufacturing

Aside from its abundance of resources, Canada also has a huge
manufacturing base, the biggest of which is the production of autos,
thanks to its ties with the U.S. motor vehicle industry. Although
Canada’s auto sector has gotten much of the spotlight, foreign investors
are keenly aware of the country’s other major producers, such as
agricultural machinery, oil and gas drilling equipment, pharmaceuticals,
high-tech electronics, and shipbuilding.

#### Services

Where Canada has recently impressed observers the most is in the
strength and stability of its financial services sector. When the world
economy tanked in 2008–09, many large international banks would have
collapsed had governments not come to their rescue with prodigious
injections of capital. Bank bailouts were particularly extensive in the
U.S., Britain, Germany, and Netherlands, and in one case, Iceland, the
banks had to be nationalized. But there was no such government
assistance for the Canadian banks. No taxpayer bailout was needed here.
No special entity had to be created to buy toxic assets.

What made Canada’s banking system stand out? First, it has always been
more tightly regulated than banks in the U.S. or Europe. For instance,
Canadian banks are not permitted to make high-risk loans, such as
adjustable-rate mortgages with five-year teaser rates, a practice that
was common in the U.S. and ended up shocking American borrowers once
rates rebounded. In contrast, when Canadian banks issued variable-rate
mortgages, they would adjust the rates daily to conform to the market.
Second, Canadian banks were better capitalized than their American and
European counterparts. Third, lenders in Canada displayed a different
management style. They were much more risk-aversive, avoiding subprime
mortgages and other less-creditworthy borrowers. Perhaps the single
biggest factor that kept the Canadian banks out of trouble was their
practice of holding on to the mortgages they originated, a policy that
prompted them to make prudent lending decisions from the start. If those
mortgages failed, the banks themselves would suffer the consequences.
But U.S. banks scoffed at such a practice. Why be cautious at all? U.S.
<span id="ch04.html_page_418"></span>lenders chose not to hold on to the
mortgages they originated. Instead, those loans were quickly packaged
with other mortgages, converted into highly complex securities, and sold
to unsuspecting investors. These concocted instruments ended up causing
an enormous real estate and mortgage bubble that eventually triggered a
historic economic and financial meltdown. Although Canada also slipped
into recession briefly in 2009, the downturn proved much less severe
than in most other countries. But what wowed many investors and
policymakers was the inherent strength of its financial sector. Canada’s
banks came to be recognized as the strongest in the world.

To be sure, Canada’s economy has some vulnerabilities. Its impressive
industrial capabilities and immense natural resources have led to a rush
of foreign investment into the country, and that has lifted the value of
the Canadian dollar to levels that have challenged exporters.

In addition, Canada’s economy is still very closely tied to the U.S.,
thanks largely to the 1989 Canada Free Trade Agreement and the 1994
North American Free Trade Agreement. Indeed, a change in interest rates
by the U.S. Federal Reserve can affect both countries, since 75% of
Canada’s exports (mostly autos and parts, agriculture products, and oil)
are destined for the U.S. Yet Canada has also taken concrete steps to
expand its trading relationship with other countries. Merchandise trade
with China, for example, has more than tripled in just the past ten
years.

For all the reasons cited above, there will continue to be growing
interest in Canada’s financial and real economy by investors. To best
track business activity in the country, one can turn to the government’s
main economic Web site, Statistics Canada. While some access to its
database requires payment, there are also several valuable sites within
Statistics Canada that are freely available.

• Main Free Site for Statistics Canada

*[www.statcan.gc.ca/start-debut-eng.html](http://www.statcan.gc.ca/start-debut-eng.html)*

• International Trade

trading areas – Seasonally adjusted, current dollars

Statistics Canada publishes a monthly summary on the country’s trade
flows around the world. It provides fresh insights into the demand that
foreigners have for Canadian goods, which can affect GDP growth,
employment, and the Canadian dollar. To access the latest trade numbers,
begin with the main Statistics Canada Web address above. Click the
listing on “International Trade,” and you arrive at a page with a
category on the left entitled “Canadian International Merchandise
Trade.” Proceed to that Web site, and you will get the most recent
statistics, with an option to view the PDF version of the report.

\(1\) The latest details on where Canadian exports are headed.

\(2\) A list of key countries and amounts that Canada imports.

\(3\) Types of commodities and finished goods that Canada exports and
imports.

<span id="ch04.html_page_419"></span><span id="ch04.html_page_420"></span>Index
of Composite Leading Indicators—Canada

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei27.jpg)

</div>

The Canadian government releases its own monthly index to forecast
economic activity. It is composed of ten components that together can
help foretell turning points in the business cycle. Four of the ten
indicators come from sources outside of Statistics Canada. They are the
Housing Index, whose source is the “Multiple Listing Services”; the TSE
300 Stock Price Index; the M1 Money Supply from the Bank of Canada; and
the U.S. Conference Board’s Index of Leading Economic Indicators.
Canada’s composite leading indicator and its ten components are smoothed
so as to reduce erratic movements. Statistics Canada uses a five-month
moving average to reduce some of the volatility in the leading index.

*[www.statcan.gc.ca/daily-quotidien/120420/dq120420b-eng.htm](http://www.statcan.gc.ca/daily-quotidien/120420/dq120420b-eng.htm)*

\(4\) The release contains the composite index and its ten components.
The composite index is presented in both smoothed form (based on a
five-month moving average) and the unsmoothed spot measure.

<span id="ch04.html_page_421"></span>• Ivey Purchasing Managers Index
(not shown)

A market-sensitive report that measures monthly changes in economic
activity based on responses from purchasing managers from across Canada.
It is conducted by the Richard Ivey School of Business at Western
University. Among the questions asked are whether purchases last month
were higher, the same, or lower than the previous month. The same basic
inquiry is made about employment, inventories, prices, and delivery
times. A diffusion index is calculated in which a number above 50 shows
an increase, whereas below 50 shows a decrease in that component.

*<http://iveypmi.uwo.ca/english/historic-data/index.htm>*

Finally, a list of available economic indicators from Statistics Canada
and when they are to be released can be found here:

*[www.statcan.gc.ca/nea-cen/dates/index-eng.htm#bop](http://www.statcan.gc.ca/nea-cen/dates/index-eng.htm#bop)*

### <span id="ch04.html_page_422"></span>Australia: Consumer Prices Retail Trade International Trade

**What Is It:** Three critical baramoters on Australia’s economic
health.

**Most Current News Release on the Internet:**

Consumer Prices:
*[www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6401.0/](http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6401.0/)*

Retail Trade:
*[www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/8501.0](http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/8501.0)*

International Trade:
*[www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/5368.0](http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/5368.0)*

**Home Web Address:** *[www.abs.gov.au/](http://www.abs.gov.au/)*

**Release Time:**

Consumer Prices: Quarterly, 11:30 a.m., local time; published the last
full week in January, April, July, and October, and refers to the
preceding quarter.

Retail Trade: Monthly, 11:30 a.m., local time; usually published the
first week of the month and covers retail sales two months earlier.

International Trade: Monthly, 11:30 a.m., local time; released the first
or second week of the month and covers trading activity two months
earlier.

**Source:** Australia Bureau of Statistics.

Only one advanced economy successfully sidestepped the 2008–09 global
financial wreckage: Australia. While the U.S. and Europe faced the worst
economic collapse since the 1930s, business “down under” just kept
humming along. In fact, the last time Australia slipped into recession
was in 1991, which means the country has enjoyed uninterrupted growth
for more than 20 years. That’s one of the longest periods of continuous
economic expansion ever recorded.

How has the country managed to pull this off? We know that the business
cycle has not been outlawed in the South Pacific. So was this
extraordinary stretch of growth due to luck—or clever design? The answer
is, a lot of both.

In terms of luck, Australia inherited several bonuses. For example,
although its cultural and geopolitical ties are firmly rooted in the
West, its geographic proximity to the world’s fastest-growing economies
enabled Australia to lock up some very lucrative trade deals. What
countries, like China and India, need most to fuel their supercharged
economies are vast quantities of raw material. And it just so happens
that Australia is well endowed with precisely the kind of natural and
industrial commodities its neighbors most need.

Australia’s well-being, however, was also the result of design. The
Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), for instance, has pursued a cautious
monetary policy. When most other central banks rushed to slash
short-term rates to near zero during the 2008–09 global
<span id="ch04.html_page_423"></span>downturn and then followed with
more unconventional forms of monetary easing, the RBA chose not to
follow suit. Instead, it pursued a more modest approach, never allowing
the benchmark cash rate to fall below 3%. That careful, deliberate
approach helped avoid the kind of debt and housing bubble that plagued
so many Western countries. Credit must also be given to Australia’s
financial institutions. Bank managers were always more conservative in
their lending practices and never succumbed to the temptation of making
a fast buck by building up excessive leverage or recklessly dishing out
mortgages, actions that brought crippling losses to Wall Street. All
that good governance by Australian banks paid off. When most of the
world was seized by a global credit crunch late in the last decade,
Aussie banks kept their strong credit ratings and thus were easily able
to raise capital to buttress their balance sheets.

Australia’s leaders also acted smartly with a well-timed economic
stimulus package to keep the economy out of trouble. Arguably the most
effective actions that set Australia on the right course were the
sweeping structural reforms introduced in the 1980s and 1990s. Those
changes loosened up the domestic economy, carefully deregulated the
financial sector, lowered import tariffs, allowed the Australian dollar
to float, and reduced barriers to allow more foreign capital into the
country. All these factors have helped insulate Australia against
economic shocks, kept the country’s jobless rate low (it helps when you
have a population of just 23 million), and provided the backdrop for a
vibrant financial services sector.

If there is one popular explanation why foreign investors have found
Australia so compelling, it is how the country has hitched its economy
to the growth prospects of China, India, Indonesia, and South Korea, and
yet still maintains large trading ties with the U.S., Japan, and the
U.K.

<div class="indent-list">

**Who are Australia’s biggest customers?**

**Eight of its ten biggest export markets are in Asia:**

**1.** China

**2.** Japan

**3.** South Korea

**4.** India

**5.** Taiwan

**6.** United States

**7.** New Zealand

**8.** Thailand

**9.** United Kingdom

**10.** Singapore

*(Based on 2010–2011 data)*

</div>

<span id="ch04.html_page_424"></span>But one also has to be careful
here. Could Australia’s economy be too dependent on the growth of its
Asian trading partners? What if economic activity slows markedly in this
region? Another concern is the large amount of foreign capital inflows.
True, it is a sign of confidence in Australia, but the flood of money
entering the country can become problematic too. By having an open
economy, capital inflows can push up the value of the Australian dollar,
drive property prices higher, and heat up inflation pressures—all of
which could slow GDP growth. This is why investors must remain vigilant
in monitoring the country’s economic statistics. The best source for
such data is the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Although they publish
hundreds of economic indicators, here are some of the most sensitive for
the financial markets:

• To begin with, you can get a quick look at Australia’s very latest
economic barometers here:

*[www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/ViewContent?readform&view=ProductsbyReleaseDate&Action=Expand&Num=1.1](http://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/ViewContent?readform&view=ProductsbyReleaseDate&Action=Expand&Num=1.1)*

• Snapshots of all its key macroeconomic indicators and their statistics
are shown on this Web page:

*[www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/1345.0](http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/1345.0)*

• Consumer Price Index (Not Shown)

Most industrial countries release CPI figures every month. Australia,
however, publishes inflation data on a quarterly basis. The government
relies on about 10,500 respondents to get 100,000 different price
quotations, and then prepares a 36-page report on retail price
inflation.

*[www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6401.0/](http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6401.0/)*

Retail Trade

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei28.jpg)

</div>

Are Australian consumers still in a spending mood? The answer has a
major influence on the stock and bond market. A sharp escalation in
expenditures can drive inflation higher and force the central bank to
act. In contrast, a dramatic and sustained slowdown in consumer outlays
can also be worrisome since it could worsen unemployment, hurt corporate
profits, and cut GDP growth. This measure compares total sales of goods
and services in retail stores in Australia (but excludes auto sales).

*[www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/mf/8501.0](http://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/mf/8501.0)*

\(1\) The 24-page retail sales report divides the data into three parts:
“Original,” which essentially represent non–seasonally adjusted numbers;
the “Seasonally Adjusted” series; and the “Trend” numbers. This last
group attempts to smooth out the monthly numbers by applying a
complicated moving average formula. Of the three, the seasonally
adjusted and trend data warrant close watching.

<span id="ch04.html_page_425"></span><span id="ch04.html_page_426"></span>(2)
Six broad retail sales categories are presented, with details on each in
the body of the report.

International Trade

<div class="image">

![Image](graphics/04sei29.jpg)

</div>

With foreign trade representing a hefty 40% of Australia’s GDP, not only
is tracking the monthly numbers on exports and imports essential to
understanding the health of the economy, it can also serve as a
forecasting tool for business activity and exchange rates.

*[www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/mf/5368.0](http://www.abs.gov.au/AUSSTATS/abs@.nsf/mf/5368.0)*

\(3\) Of particular interest are the swings in trade with its key
partners, given the dominant role they play in Australia’s overall trade

thousands of dollars to churn out statistics on the U.S. and
international economies. Today, thanks to the Internet and the intense
competition among financial services companies to attract customers,
anyone can easily obtain economic or financial data directly from the
Web at no cost. This chapter lists online resources that provide such
information free.

of thinking that gives an edge—an idea that opens new\

that simply helps make sense of it all.

We work with leading authors in the various arenas\
of business and finance to bring cutting-edge thinking\
and best-learning practices to a global market.

It is our goal to create world-class print publications\
and electronic products that give readers\
knowledge and understanding that can then be\
applied, whether studying or at work.
